A categorical framework for congruence of applicative bisimilarity in higher-order languages
Tom Hirschowitz ORCID:0000-0002-7220-4067, Ambroise Lafont ORCID:0000-0002-9299-641X

Abstract
. Applicative bisimilarity is a coinductive characterisation of observational equivalence in call-by-name lambda-calculus, introduced by Abramsky (1990). Howe (1996) gave a direct proof that it is a congruence, and generalised the result to all languages complying with a suitable format. We propose a categorical framework for specifying operational semantics, in which we prove that (an abstract analogue of) applicative bisimilarity is automatically a congruence. Example instances include standard applicative bisimilarity in call-by-name, call-by-value, and call-by-name non-deterministic λ \lambda -calculus, and more generally all languages complying with a variant of Howe’s format.

1.
Introduction

1.1.
Motivation

This paper is a contribution to the search for efficient and
high-level mathematical tools to specify and reason about programming
languages. This search arguably goes back at least to Turi and
Plotkin
[
plotkin:turi:bialgebraic
]
, who coined the name
“Mathematical Operational Semantics”, and proved a general congruence
theorem for bisimilarity. This approach has been deeply investigated,
notably for quantitative languages
[
Bartels
]
. However, as of
today, attempts to apply it to higher-order (e.g., functional)
languages have failed.

In previous
work
[
hirschowitz:hal-01815328
,
hirschowitz:hal-02273790
]
, the
first author has proposed an alternative approach to the problem,
dropping the coalgebraic notion of bisimulation used by Turi and
Plotkin in favour of a notion based on factorisation systems, similar
to Joyal et al.’s
[
DBLP:conf/lics/JoyalNW93
]
. Furthermore,
congruence of bisimilarity is notably obtained by assuming that syntax
induces a
familial
monad
[
Diers1978Spectres
,
DBLP:journals/mscs/CarboniJ95
,
Weber:famfun
]
.

However, the new approach has only been applied to simple, first-order
languages like the

\pi
-calculus
[
Milner:pi
,
DBLP:books/daglib/0004377
]
, and Positive
GSOS specifications
[
GSOS
]
. In this paper, we extend it to
functional languages, notably covering the paradigmatic case of

applicative
bisimilarity
[
Applicative
]
in call-by-name and
call-by-value
\lambda
-calculus, as well as in a simple, non-deterministic

\lambda
-calculus
[
DavideLazy
,
DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96
, §7]
. We
even show that our framework subsumes the general, syntactic format
proposed by Howe
[
DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96
, Lemma 6.1]
. We thus obtain
for the first time a generic, categorical congruence result for
applicative bisimilarity in functional languages.

1.2.
Overview

A bit more precisely:

•

We propose a simple notion of signature for programming
languages.

•

Each signature has a category of models, including an initial
one, intuitively its operational semantics.

•

An abstract analogue of applicative bisimilarity, called

substitution-closed
bisimilarity, may be defined in any
model, and in particular in the initial one.

•

Under suitable hypotheses, we show that substitution-closed
bisimilarity is a congruence in the initial model.

Categorically, this unfolds as follows.

(i)

We define an abstract notion of (labelled)
transition systems, as objects of a category
\mathbf{C}
, in such a way that

•

there is a forgetful functor
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}_{0}
, intuitively returning
the (potentially structured) set of states of a transition system;

•

bisimulation and bisimilarity may be defined for any
transition system.

(ii)

Adopting Fiore, Plotkin, and Turi’s seminal
framework
[
fiore:presheaf
,
DBLP:conf/lics/Fiore08
]
, we then
assume that
\mathbf{C}_{0}
is monoidal, and define models of the syntax to be

monoid algebras
for a given
pointed strong
endofunctor

\Sigma_{0}
on
\mathbf{C}_{0}
. Monoid algebras, a.k.a.
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids, are

\Sigma_{0}
-algebras equipped with compatible monoid structure, which
models capture-avoiding substitution. The category
\Sigma_{0}\mon
of

\Sigma_{0}
-monoids has an initial object
\mathbf{Z}_{0}
, whose carrier is the free

\Sigma_{0}
-algebra on the monoidal unit
I
, as we prove in
Coq
[
BHLcode
]
. In all examples,
\mathbf{Z}_{0}
is precisely the syntax.

(iii)

This category
\Sigma_{0}\mon
induces by pullback a category
\Sigma_{0}\Trans

of transition systems whose states are equipped with
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
structure. We call these
transition monoid algebras
, or

transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids
, or even simply

transition monoids
when
\Sigma_{0}
is the identity. The relevant
notions of bisimulation and bisimilarity for such objects are
defined as in
(i)
, but for
substitution-closed

relations.

(iv)

We then define models of the dynamics to be certain algebras,
called
vertical
, for an endofunctor on
\Sigma_{0}\Trans
. There is an
initial vertical algebra
\mathbf{Z}
, which in examples is the syntactic
transition system. (Furthermore, standard applicative bisimilarity coincides
with substitution-closed bisimilarity.)

(v)

Finally, following an abstract analogue of Howe’s method, we
show that, under suitable hypotheses, substitution-closed
bisimilarity on
\mathbf{Z}
is a congruence. One crucial hypothesis is

cellularity
, in a sense closely related
to
[
garner:hal-01246365
]
.

1.3.
Related work

Plotkin and Turi’s
bialgebraic
semantics

[
plotkin:turi:bialgebraic
]
and its few
variants
[
DBLP:journals/tcs/CorradiniHM02
,
DBLP:conf/lics/Staton08
]

prove abstract congruence theorems for bisimilarity. However, they do
not cover higher-order languages like the
\lambda
-calculus, let alone
applicative bisimilarity. This was one of the main motivations for our
work. Among more recent work, quite some inspiration was drawn from
Ahrens et al.
[
AHLM19
,
HHL
]
, notably in the use of vertical
algebras. However, a difference is that we do not insist that
transitions be stable under substitution. In a different direction,
Dal Lago et al.
[
DBLP:conf/lics/LagoGL17
]
prove a general
congruence theorem for applicative bisimilarity, for a
\lambda
-calculus
with algebraic effects. As briefly discussed in the conclusion, our
framework does not yet account for such results. However, it places
the generality in a different direction: namely, it is not tied to any
particular language (like the
\lambda
-calculus
in
[
DBLP:conf/lics/LagoGL17
]
). It would of course be useful to
find a common generalisation.

Links with other relevant work by, e.g., Bodin et
al.
[
DBLP:journals/pacmpl/BodinGJS19
]
, though desirable, remain
unclear, perhaps because of the very different methods used.

Furthermore, the cellularity used here is close to but different from
the
\mathbf{T}_{s}^{\vee}
-familiality of
[
hirschowitz:hal-01815328
]
. It would be
instructive to better understand potential links between the two.
Finally, let us mention recent work which, just like ours, strives to
establish abstract versions of standard constructions and theorems in
programming language theory like type
soundness
[
DBLP:conf/lics/ArkorF20
]
or
gluing
[
Fiore02
,
DBLP:conf/lics/FioreS20
,
DBLP:conf/fossacs/FioreS20
]
.

1.4.
Relation to conference version

This paper is a bit more than a journal version of our previous
work
[
BHL
]
. Here is a brief summary of changes.

(a)

In
[
BHL
]
, we work with a non-trivial generalisation of
monoid algebras to
skew monoidal
categories
[
Szlachanyi
]

and
structurally strong
functors. Here, by giving a better
type to
\Sigma_{1}
, the endofunctor for specifying the dynamics, we manage
to work with standard monoid algebras. This has the additional
advantages of

•

avoiding a slightly
ad hoc
compositionality assumption
of
[
BHL
]
, and

•

relaxing the requirement that the tensor product should be
familial.

(b)

In
[
BHL
]
, because Howe’s closure operates only at
the level of states, we work mostly with

prebisimulations
, in the sense
of
[
hirschowitz:hal-01815328
, §5.1]
. This notion is designed
to detect when the state part of a relation underlies a
bisimulation, regardless of what it does on transitions. However,
it feels more
ad hoc
than the standard definition of
bisimulation by lifting
[
DBLP:conf/lics/JoyalNW93
]
. In this
paper, we extend Howe’s closure to transitions, thus avoiding
prebisimulations entirely.

(c)

In
[
BHL
]
, we rely on directed unions of relations, which
leads to quite a few, rather painful proofs by induction. Here, we
use higher-level methods to construct Howe’s closure, essentially
through categorification and algebraicisation. Namely:

(1)

We define bisimilarity as the final object not in some
partially-ordered set of relations as usual, but in some category
of spans (see also
[
DBLP:conf/calco/BasoldPR17
]
).

(2)

Furthermore, we define Howe’s closure directly as a free
monoid algebra for a suitable pointed strong endofunctor on spans.

(3)

More generally, we systematically rely on universal
properties, which simplifies a significant number of proofs.

(d)

We put less emphasis on cellularity, viewing it only as a
sufficient condition for a perhaps more natural hypothesis, which
already appeared in a slightly different form
in
[
DBLP:conf/lics/Staton08
]
, namely the fact that
\Sigma_{1}

preserves functional bisimulations.

(e)

We obtain a congruence theorem of similar scope
(Theorem
), and cover three new, detailed applications
(§
): call-by-value, big-step
\lambda
-calculus (which
was covered but too naively in
[
BHL
]
, as we explain), a
call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus with unary, erratic choice
from
[
DavideLazy
, §7]
, and a general format proposed by
Howe
[
DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96
, Lemma 6.1]
.

(f)

We fill a gap in the proof of
[
BHL
, Lemma 5.13]
, by
requiring the endofunctor
\Sigma_{0}
for specifying the dynamics to
preserve sifted colimits (see Remark
35
).

1.5.
Plan

In §
2
, we start by briefly recalling call-by-name

\lambda
-calculus and applicative bisimilarity. We then explain how to view
the latter as substitution-closed bisimilarity, and sketch Howe’s
method. In §
3
, we then give a brief overview of the
new framework by example, including a recap on monoid algebras and a
statement of the main theorem (in the considered case). We then dive
into the technical core of the paper by presenting our framework for
transition systems and bisimilarity (§
4
), operational
semantics (§
5
), and then substitution-closed
bisimilarity and the main result (Theorem
), together
with a high-level proof sketch (§
).
In §
, we reformulate the main hypothesis of
Theorem
using cellularity, which allows us to use
well-known results from weak factorisation systems as sufficient
conditions. We then apply our results to examples
in §
. The full proof of
Theorem
is given in §
. Finally, we
conclude and give some perspectives on future work in §
.

1.6.
Notation and preliminaries

In this subsection, we fix some basic notation, and review some
preliminaries.

1.6.1.
Basic notation

We often conflate natural numbers
n\in\mathbb{N}
with the corresponding sets

\{1,\ldots,n\}
. For all sets
X
and objects
C
of a given category,
we denote by
X\cdot C
the
X
-fold coproduct of
C
with itself, i.e.,

\sum_{x\in X}C
. Let
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}
denote the category of (directed, multi)
graphs,
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}
the category of small categories, and
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}
the category
of locally small categories.

1.6.2.
Comma categories and lax limits

Given functors
F\colon\mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}
and
G\colon\mathbf{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}
,
the
comma
category
F/G
has

•

as objects all triples
(A,B,\varphi)
, where
A\in\mathbf{A}
,
B\in\mathbf{B}
,
and
\varphi\colon F(A)\rightarrow G(B)
, and

•

as morphisms
(A,B,\varphi)\rightarrow(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime})
all pairs of morphisms

u\colon A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
and
v\colon B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
making the following square commute.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(A^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(B^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle F(u)
\scriptstyle\varphi
\scriptstyle G(v)
\scriptstyle\varphi^{\prime}

We have the following well-known fact:

Proposition 1
.

If
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
have, and
F
preserves colimits of any given shape,
then the projection functor
F/G\rightarrow\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}
creates them.

Symmetrically, if
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
have, and
G
preserves limits of any
given shape, then the projection functor
F/G\rightarrow\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}
creates them.

The comma category
F/G
is well-known
[
Kelly89
,
TwoToposes
]

to be the universal category equipped with projections to

\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
and a natural transformation as in the following
diagram.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F/G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{C}}
\scriptstyle F
\scriptstyle G

Kelly
[
Kelly89
]
explains that the comma category is a kind of
lax limit of
F
and
G
. When
F
is an identity, we call the
comma category a
lax limit
of
G
.

1.6.3.
Presheaves

Let
\widehat{\mathbb{C}}
denote the category of (contravariant) presheaves on
\mathbb{C}
,
and
\mathbf{y}\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}
the Yoneda embedding, mapping
c
to
\mathbb{C}(-,c)
.
Given a presheaf
F\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}}
, an element
x\in F(c)
, and a morphism

c\xrightarrow{f}c^{\prime}
, we sometimes denote
F(f)(x)
by
x\cdot f
. Given two
categories
\mathbb{C}_{1}
and
\mathbb{C}_{2}
, we denote by
[\mathbb{C}_{1},\mathbb{C}_{2}]
the functor category
between them.

1.6.4.
Spans and relations

In a category
\mathbf{C}
with binary products, we interchangeably use spans

X\leftarrow R\rightarrow Y
and their pairings
R\rightarrow X\times Y
, sometimes also calling the
latter spans. Spans from
X
to
Y
are the objects of a category

\mathit{Span}(\mathbf{C})(X,Y)
, which is isomorphic to the slice category
\mathbf{C}/X\times Y
in
the presence of binary products. When
\mathbf{C}
has pullbacks, these
categories are the hom-categories of a bicategory
[
Benabou
]

\mathit{Span}(\mathbf{C})
, in which composition of morphisms is given by pullback. A

relation
from
X
to
Y
is merely a span whose pairing

R\rightarrow X\times Y
is monic.

{defi}

A
strong epimorphism
is a morphism with the strong left
lifting property w.r.t. all monomorphisms, i.e., a morphism

e\colon A\rightarrow B
such that for all (solid) commuting squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle e
\scriptstyle k
\scriptstyle m

with
m
monic there exists a unique lifting
k
making both
triangles commute.

The terminology is justified by the following result.

Lemma 2
.

In a category with equalisers, any strong epimorphism is an
epimorphism.

Proof 1.1
.

Let us assume that
e\colon A\rightarrow B
is a strong epi and
fe=ge
, with

f,g\colon B\rightarrow C
. Then, let
k\colon A^{\prime}\rightarrow B
denote the equaliser of
f
and

g
. Because
e
equalises
f
and
g
, it factors as
kh
, for some
unique
h\colon A\rightarrow A^{\prime}
. But now
k
is monic, so by lifting there is a
unique
l
making both triangles commute in the following diagram.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle h
\scriptstyle e
\scriptstyle l
\scriptstyle k

We thus have

f=f\circ\id_{B}=f\circ k\circ l=g\circ k\circ l=g\circ\id_{B}=g.

The morphism
e
is thus epi, as claimed.

Corollary 3
.

Factoring a morphism as a strong epi followed by a mono
yields an image.

Proof 1.2
.

Initiality is directly given by the lifting property.

Proposition 4
.

In any locally finitely presentable category, images always exist,
and may be computed as (strong epi, mono)-factorisations.

Proof 1.3
.

This is (part of)
[
Adamek
, Proposition 1.61]
.

Let us finally observe:

Proposition 5
.

In locally presentable category, unions of subobjects
exist, and may be computed by taking the cotupling of all considered
subobjects, and then their (strong epi, mono)-factorisation.

Proof 1.4
.

Straightforward.

1.6.6.
Initial algebras

Any finitary endofunctor
F
on any cocomplete category admits
by

an initial algebra, which we denote
by
\mathbf{Z}_{F}
. Although this is detailed below, we prefer to avoid
confusion and warn the reader that we also use
\mathbf{Z}_{F}
for the initial

F
-monoid, for any
pointed strong
endofunctor

on any nice

Throughout the paper, when not explicitly attached to any

shorthand for

(see, e.g., Proposition

).

1.6.7.
Weak factorisation systems

Finally, let us fix some notation about weak factorisation systems.
In any category
\mathscr{C}
, we say that a morphism
f\colon A\rightarrow B
has the (weak)
left lifting property w.r.t.
g\colon C\rightarrow D
when for all commuting
squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}}
\scriptstyle u
\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle v
\scriptstyle k
\scriptstyle g

there is a lifting
k
as shown that makes both triangles commute.
Equivalently, we say that
g
has the right lifting property w.r.t.
f
, and write
f\mathrel{\pitchfork}g
. Given a fixed set
\mathbb{J}
of morphisms,
the set of morphisms
g
such that
j\mathrel{\pitchfork}g
for all
j\in\mathbb{J}

is denoted by
\mathbb{J}^{\pitchfork}
. Similarly, the set of morphisms
f
such that

f\mathrel{\pitchfork}j
for all
j\in\mathbb{J}
is denoted by
{{}^{\pitchfork}{\mathbb{J}}}
. In
particular, if
f\in{{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}}
and
g\in{\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork}
, then

f\mathrel{\pitchfork}g
. If
\mathscr{C}
is locally presentable
[
Adamek
]
, then

({{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}},\mathbb{J}^{\pitchfork})
forms a
weak factorisation system
, in
the sense that additionally any morphism
f\colon X\rightarrow Y
factors as

X\xrightarrow{l}Z\xrightarrow{r}Y
with
l\in{{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}}
and
r\in\mathbb{J}^{\pitchfork}

(see
[
Hovey
, Theorem 2.1.14]
). Morphisms in
\mathbb{J}^{\pitchfork}
are
generically called
fibrations
, while morphisms in

{{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}}
are called
cofibrations
.

Let us conclude with the following easy, yet helpful result.

Lemma 6
.

For any locally finitely presentable category and set
\mathbb{J}
of maps
therein, if the domains and codomains of maps in
\mathbb{J}
are finitely
presentable, then fibrations are closed under filtered colimits in
the arrow category.

Proof 1.5
.

Let us consider any given filtered diagram
(f_{i}\colon A_{i}\rightarrow B_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{D}}

of fibrations, and a colimit
f\colon A\rightarrow B
in the arrow category, say

\mathbf{C}^{\rightarrow}
. We must show that
j\mathrel{\pitchfork}f
for all
j\in\mathbb{J}
. Let
us thus consider any given commuting square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle u
\scriptstyle j
\scriptstyle v
\scriptstyle f

with
j\in\mathbb{J}
. Colimits in the arrow category are pointwise, so

A=\colim_{i}A_{i}
and
B=\colim_{i}B_{i}
. Thus, by finite
presentability of
X
and

, and by filteredness of the diagram

\mathbb{D}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}
,
u
and
v
factor through some
A_{i_{0}}
and
B_{i_{1}}
,
respectively. By filteredness of the diagram again, w.l.o.g., we
may take
i_{0}=i_{1}
, such that
(u,v)\colon j\rightarrow f
factors through

f_{i_{0}}
.
But because
f_{i_{0}}
is a fibration, we find a lifting as
in
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{i_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{i_{0}}}

which provides the desired lifting for the original square.

2.
A brief review of Howe’s method

2.1.
Applicative bisimilarity

Let us consider the standard, big-step presentation of call-by-name

\lambda
-calculus:

\frac{}{\lambda x.e\Downarrow\lambda x.e}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow\lambda x.e^{\prime}_{1}\quad e^{\prime}_{1}[x\mapsto e_{2}]\Downarrow e_{3}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow e_{3}}

Standardly, the evaluation relation
\Downarrow
is considered between closed
terms only.

Applicative bisimilarity is an important notion of program equivalence
in this language. Indeed, it is coinductive, so one may prove that any
two given programs are applicative bisimilar merely by exhibiting an
applicative bisimulation. Furthermore, it is sound and complete
w.r.t. (i.e., it coincides with) standard contextual equivalence.

Let us briefly recall the definition. Applicative bisimilarity is
standardly introduced in two stages, which we now recall.

{defiC}
[
[
Applicative
, Definition 2.3]
]
A relation
R
over closed
\lambda
-terms is an
applicative
simulation
iff
e_{1}\mathrel{R}e_{2}
and
e_{1}\Downarrow\lambda x.e^{\prime}_{1}
entail
the existence of
e^{\prime}_{2}
such that
e_{2}\Downarrow\lambda x.e^{\prime}_{2}
and, for all terms

e
,
e^{\prime}_{1}[x\mapsto e]\mathrel{R}e^{\prime}_{2}[x\mapsto e]
.

An
applicative bisimulation
is an applicative simulation
R

whose converse, say
R^{\dagger}
, is also an applicative simulation.

Applicative bisimulations are closed under unions, and so there is a
largest applicative bisimulation, called
applicative
bisimilarity
and denoted by
\sim
.

Then comes the second stage:

{defi}

The
open extension
of a relation
R
on closed terms is the
relation
R^{\otimes}
on potentially open terms such that

e\mathrel{R^{\otimes}}e^{\prime}
iff for all closed substitutions
\sigma
covering
all involved free variables we have
e[\sigma]\mathrel{R}e^{\prime}[\sigma]
.

Let us readily notice the following alternative characterisation of
open extension.

{defi}

A relation
S
on open terms is
substitution-closed
iff for
all
e\mathrel{S}e^{\prime}
and (potentially open) substitutions
\sigma
, we
have
e[\sigma]\mathrel{S}e^{\prime}[\sigma]
.

Lemma 7
.

The open extension of any relation
R
is the greatest

substitution-closed
relation contained in
R
on closed
terms.

Proof 2.1
.

Let us first show that
R^{\otimes}
is substitution-closed. For any

e_{1}\mathrel{R^{\otimes}}e_{2}
and
\sigma
, we want to show

e_{1}[\sigma]\mathrel{R^{\otimes}}e_{2}[\sigma]
. For this, we in turn need to show that
for all closing substitutions
\gamma
, we have

e_{1}[\sigma][\gamma]\mathrel{R}e_{2}[\sigma][\gamma]
. But
e_{i}[\sigma][\gamma]=e_{i}[\sigma[\gamma]]
, where
by definition and
\sigma[\gamma](x)=\sigma(x)[\gamma]
. Furthermore,
\sigma[\gamma]
is closing. So,
because we have
e_{1}\mathrel{R^{\otimes}}e_{2}
, by definition of open extension, we
get
e_{1}[\sigma][\gamma]\mathrel{R}e_{2}[\sigma][\gamma]
as desired.

Let us now show that
R^{\otimes}
is the greatest substitution-closed
relation contained in
R
on closed terms. For this, consider any
substitution-closed
R^{\prime}
contained in
R
on closed terms: for all

e\mathrel{R^{\prime}}e^{\prime}
, by substitution-closedness, we have

e[\sigma]\mathrel{R^{\prime}}e^{\prime}[\sigma]
for all closing
\sigma
. So because
R^{\prime}
is
contained in
R
on closed terms, we further have

e[\sigma]\mathrel{R}e^{\prime}[\sigma]
. This proves
e\mathrel{R^{\otimes}}e^{\prime}
, and
thus
R^{\prime}\subseteq R^{\otimes}
as desired.

The result we wish to abstract over is the following
(see
[
Pitts:howe
]
for a historical account).

Theorem 8
.

The open extension
\sim^{\otimes}
of applicative bisimilarity is a congruence:
it is an equivalence relation, and furthermore it is context-closed, i.e.,

•

e_{1}\mathrel{\sim^{\otimes}}e_{2}
entails
\lambda x.e_{1}\mathrel{\sim^{\otimes}}\lambda x.e_{2}
for all
x
;

•

e_{1}\mathrel{\sim^{\otimes}}e_{2}
and
e^{\prime}_{1}\mathrel{\sim^{\otimes}}e^{\prime}_{2}
entail

e_{1}\ e^{\prime}_{1}\mathrel{\sim^{\otimes}}e_{2}\ e^{\prime}_{2}
.

Proving that
\sim^{\otimes}
is an equivalence relation is in fact straightforward.
In the following, we focus on the context-closedness property.

2.2.
Howe’s method

Howe’s method for proving Theorem
8
consists in
considering a suitable relation
\sim^{\bullet}
, closed under substitution and
context, and containing
\sim^{\otimes}
by construction. He then shows that this
relation
\sim^{\bullet}
is an applicative bisimulation. By maximality of
\sim^{\otimes}
,
we thus also have
{\sim^{\bullet}}\subseteq{\sim^{\otimes}}
hence both relations coincide and

\sim^{\otimes}
is context-closed as desired. However, as explained
in
[
BHL
, §5.1]
, the presence of a substitution in the premises of
a transition rule seems to require
{\sim^{\bullet}}
to be closed under

heterogeneous
substitution, in the sense that, e.g., if

e_{1}\sim^{\bullet}e^{\prime}_{1}
and
e_{2}\sim^{\bullet}e^{\prime}_{2}
(for open terms), then

e_{1}[x\mapsto e_{2}]\sim^{\bullet}e^{\prime}_{1}[x\mapsto e^{\prime}_{2}]
. The problem is that building this into the
definition of
\sim^{\bullet}
leads to difficulties in the proof that it is an
applicative bisimulation. Howe’s workaround consists in requiring
\sim^{\bullet}
to be
closed under sequential composition with
\sim^{\otimes}
from the outset.
Coupling this right action with context closedness, he thus defines

\sim^{\bullet}
as the smallest context-closed relation satisfying the rules

\frac{}{x\sim^{\bullet}x}\frac{e\sim^{\bullet}e^{\prime}\quad e^{\prime}\sim^{\otimes}e^{\prime\prime}}{e\sim^{\bullet}e^{\prime\prime}}~\cdot

By construction,
\sim^{\bullet}
is reflexive and context-closed. By
induction, it also substitution-closed. Furthermore, by reflexivity
and the second rule, it also contains
\sim^{\otimes}
, and finally the second
rule clearly entails
{\sim^{\bullet}};{\sim^{\otimes}}\subseteq{\sim^{\bullet}}
, where “
;
” denotes
relational (or sequential) composition. It takes an induction to
prove stability under heterogeneous substitution, but to give a feel
for it, in the basic case where
e_{1}\sim^{\otimes}e^{\prime}_{1}
, we have

e_{1}[x\mapsto e_{2}]\sim^{\bullet}e_{1}[x\mapsto e^{\prime}_{2}]\sim^{\otimes}e^{\prime}_{1}[x\mapsto e^{\prime}_{2}]

by context closedness of
\sim^{\bullet}

and substitution closedness of
\sim^{\otimes}
, so we conclude by

{\sim^{\bullet}};{\sim^{\otimes}}\subseteq{\sim^{\bullet}}
.

The initial plan was to show that
\sim^{\bullet}
is an applicative bisimulation
and deduce that it coincides with
\sim^{\otimes}
. It can in fact be slightly
optimised by first showing that
\sim^{\bullet}
is an applicative simulation,
and then that its transitive closure
(\sim^{\bullet})^{+}
is
symmetric.
The relation
(\sim^{\bullet})^{+}
is also an applicative
simulation, hence by symmetry an applicative bisimulation. This entails
the last inclusion in the chain
{\sim^{\otimes}}\subseteq{\sim^{\bullet}}\subseteq{(\sim^{\bullet})^{+}}\subseteq{\sim^{\otimes}},

showing that all relations coincide. Finally, because
\sim^{\bullet}
is
context-closed, so is
\sim^{\otimes}
, as desired.

2.3.
Non-standard presentation

The above, standard evaluation rules for call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus are
not directly compatible with our framework. We thus adopt a slightly
different presentation, where the evaluation relation relates closed
terms to terms with just one potential free variable. The problem and
its solution should become clear in §
, where we
investigate Howe’s general format
[
DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96
, Lemma 6.1]
.
There, we show that any language complying with Howe’s format may be
covered by our framework, up to suitable encoding. The present,
non-standard presentation is a slight variant of this encoding,
optimised for
\lambda
-calculus.
The new transition rules are as follows.

\frac{}{\lambda x.e\Downarrow e}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow e^{\prime}_{1}\quad e^{\prime}_{1}[e_{2}]\Downarrow e_{3}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow e_{3}}

Here
e^{\prime}_{1}[e_{2}]
denotes substitution of the unique potential free
variable in
e^{\prime}_{1}
by
e_{2}
. We will see below that, with this
transition system, the essentially standard notion of bisimulation
coupled with the substitution-closedness requirement yields
applicative bisimilarity.

3.
Overview by example

In this section, we describe one particular instance of our framework,
which models call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus.

3.1.
Syntax

Let us first define the syntax of
\lambda
-calculus,
following
[
fiore:presheaf
]
, as an initial
1
1

1

This pattern
is advocated by the approach of
initial algebra
semantics

[
InitialSemantics
]
, where initiality provides a
recursion principle.
object in a suitable category of models. Very
roughly, a model of

should be satisfied, e.g.,

(e_{1}\ e_{2})[\sigma]=e_{1}[\sigma]\ e_{2}[\sigma]\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}

(1)

A natural setting for specifying such operations is the functor
category
\mathbf{C}_{0}:=[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]

\Sigma_{\Lambda}(X)(n)=X(n+1)+X(n)^{2}.

(2)

Let us now consider substitution. The idea here is to equip

•

2
2

2

In

;

•

Being equipped with substitution (and variables) is thus

Finally, how do we enforce equations such as (

This goes in two stages:

•

Let us first explain the notion of pointed strength.

Application:

For modelling Equation (
1

Abstraction:

The equation is then

\lambda(e)[\sigma]=\lambda(e[\sigma^{\uparrow}]).

(3)

All in all, we have:

{defi}

modulo the equivalence

(f\cdot k)\Lparen e_{1},\ldots,e_{q}\Rparen\sim k\Lparen e_{f(1)},\ldots,e_{f(p)}\Rparen\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}

The first rule is the standard rule for variables, while the second

.

3.2.
Transition systems and bisimilarity

The appropriate notion of transition system for
\lambda
-calculus
is as follows.

{defi}

A
transition system

X
consists of

•

a
state object

X_{0}\in\mathbf{C}_{0}=[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
,

•

a set

of

, and

•

giving the source and target of

).

Transition systems form a category

, whose morphisms

consist of compatible morphisms

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}(0)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}(0)}
\scriptstyle f_{1}
\scriptstyle s_{X}
\scriptstyle f_{0}
\scriptstyle s_{Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}(1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}(1)}
\scriptstyle f_{1}
\scriptstyle t_{X}
\scriptstyle f_{0}
\scriptstyle t_{Y}
{nota}

We write

for

such that

.

{exa}
The
syntactic

Our next goal is to introduce bisimulation, for which it is convenient
to characterise

as a presheaf category. This characterisation may

the same reason as graphs do. Here is the base category:

{defi}

Let

denote the category obtained by augmenting

with an

\Downarrow
, together with morphisms

, and

More concretely:

•

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Downarrow}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

\scriptstyle s_{\Downarrow}

\scriptstyle!

Proposition 11
.

Transition systems are isomorphic to covariant presheaves on
\mathbb{F}[\Downarrow]
.

{nota}

We often implicitly convert from transition systems to covariant
presheaves, and conversely.

Proof 3.1

(Proof sketch)
.

This will be proved below by abstract means, but for intuition let us
sketch the correspondence. Given a transition system

\langle s_{X},t_{X}\rangle\colon X_{1}\rightarrow X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)
, we construct a presheaf
X^{\prime}
by
setting

•

X^{\prime}(n)=X_{0}(n)
for all
n\in\mathbb{F}
,

•

X^{\prime}(\Downarrow)=X_{1}
,

•

with the action of
s_{\Downarrow},t_{\Downarrow}\in\mathbb{F}
given by
s_{X}
and
t_{X}
,

•

inducing the action of all
s_{\Downarrow,n}
and
t_{\Downarrow,n,i}
by composition.

Conversely, for any presheaf
Y
, we construct a transition system
Y^{\prime}
defined as follows:

•

the state object
Y^{\prime}_{0}\in[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
is given by restriction of

Y
;

•

the set
Y^{\prime}_{1}
of transitions is
Y(\Downarrow)
;

•

and
s_{Y^{\prime}}
and
t_{Y^{\prime}}
are
Y(s_{\Downarrow})
and
Y(t_{\Downarrow})
,
respectively.

The correspondence yields basic, graph-like examples of transition
systems.

{exa}

(a)

The representable presheaf
\mathbf{y}_{0}
associated to
0\in\mathbb{F}
has a
single closed state
k_{0}
and its renamings (i.e.,
(\mathbf{y}_{0})_{0}(n)=1

for all

and for transitions
(\mathbf{y}_{0})_{1}=\emptyset
).

(b)

The representable presheaf
\mathbf{y}_{\Downarrow}
consists of a closed state

k_{0}
, a state

with one free variable, their renamings, and a

.

(c)

Let
\mathbf{y}_{s_{\Downarrow}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{\Downarrow}
denote the morphism mapping
k_{0}
to

k_{0}
.

Using these basic examples, we may define bisimulation and
bisimilarity by lifting following
[
DBLP:conf/lics/JoyalNW93
]
:

{defi}

A morphism

in
\mathbf{C}
is a

when
it has the right lifting property w.r.t. the source map

\mathbf{y}_{s_{\Downarrow}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{1}
. A span

is a

when its
left leg

is a functional bisimulation, and a

when both legs are.

Remark 12
.

In this case, the Yoneda lemma says that
\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}_{0},X)\cong X_{0}(0)
and

\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}_{\Downarrow},Y)\cong Y_{1}
. The right lifting property for a morphism

thus says that given any

whose source

is

for some

, there exists

such that

and

, which matches the
usual definition of functional bisimulation. The following diagram
might help readability.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{y}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{y}_{\Downarrow}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle x
\scriptstyle s_{\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle e
\scriptstyle e^{\prime}
\scriptstyle f

{defi}

Let
\mathbf{B}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{s}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{m}(X,Y)
denote the category of bisimulations, with span
morphisms between them.

Proposition 13
.

\mathbf{B}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{s}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{m}(X,Y)
has a terminal object, called
bisimilarity
and
denoted by
\sim_{X,Y}
.

{exa}

Bisimilarity on the syntactic transition system merely amounts
to simultaneous convergence, because evaluation returns an open
term, which does not have any further transition. In this case, a
more relevant behavioural equivalence is substitution-closed
bisimilarity, which we will define below.

3.3.
Operational semantics

Just as we have defined the syntax as an initial
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
(Example
3.1
), let us now define the dynamics by
initiality, again starting by finding the right notion of model.
First of all, models will be found among transition systems
X
whose
underlying presheaf
X_{0}\in[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
is a
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid. Let us give these
a name.

{defi}

A
transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
is a transition system
X
,
together with
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid structure on its vertices (a.k.a. states)
object
X_{0}
. When
\Sigma_{0}=\id
, we call transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids
simply
transition monoids
. (Any transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid is
thus in particular a transition monoid.)

Let
\Sigma_{0}\Trans
denote the category of transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids, with as
morphisms all transition system morphisms which induce
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
morphisms on vertices objects.

The idea is to model the transition rules as an endofunctor on
transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids, leaving the underlying
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid untouched,
i.e., a functor making the triangle
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}\Trans}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}\Trans}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}\mon}
\scriptstyle\Sigma_{1}
\scriptstyle\mathscr{D}
\scriptstyle\mathscr{D}

commute, where
\mathscr{D}
denotes the forgetful functor (i.e.,
\mathscr{D}(X)=X_{0}
).

For call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus, the functor
\Sigma_{1}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans

modelling the non-standard rules at the end of §
2
is
defined as follows.

•

On states, commutation of the above triangle imposes

\Sigma_{1}(X)_{0}=X_{0}
.

•

On transitions, let

\Sigma_{1}(X)_{1}=X_{0}(1)+A_{\beta}(X)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}

where
A_{\beta}(X)
denotes the set of valid premises for the
second rule in §
2.3
, i.e., triples
(r_{1},e_{2},r_{2})

such that

–

r_{1},r_{2}\in X_{1}
are transitions,

–

e_{2}\in X_{0}(0)
is a state, and

–

r_{2}\cdot s_{\Downarrow}=(r_{1}\cdot t_{\Downarrow})[e_{2}]
, i.e., the source
r_{2}\cdot s_{\Downarrow}
of
r_{2}
is
obtained by substituting
e_{2}
for the unique free variable in the target of

r_{1}
.

In other words:

\frac{\frac{r_{1}}{e_{1}\Downarrow e^{\prime}_{1}}\quad\frac{r_{2}}{e^{\prime}_{1}[e_{2}]\Downarrow e_{3}}\quad}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow e_{3}}~\cdot

Let us notice that substitution here follows from the monoid
structure of
X
.

•

We then define the source and target maps:

–

for the first term
X_{0}(1)
,

*

the source of any

is
\lambda_{1}(e)
, where

\lambda_{n}\colon X_{0}(n+1)\rightarrow X_{0}(n)
follows from the
\Sigma_{0}
-algebra
structure of
X_{0}
;

*

the target is

itself;

–

for the second term
A_{\beta}(X)
,

*

the source of any
in_{2}(r_{1},e_{2},r_{2})
is
(r_{1}\cdot s_{\Downarrow})\ e_{2}
, i.e., the
application of the source of
r_{1}
to
e_{2}
(again using the

\Sigma_{0}
-algebra structure of
X_{0}
);

*

the target is
r_{2}\cdot t_{\Downarrow}
.

Accordingly, our notion of model is the following.

{defi}

A
vertical
\Sigma_{1}
-algebra
is a transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
X

equipped with a morphism
\nu_{X}\colon\Sigma_{1}(X)\rightarrow X
such that

\mathscr{D}(\nu_{X})=\id_{X_{0}}
, or equivalently a map
(\nu_{X})_{1}
making the following
triangle commute.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{1}(X)_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)}
\scriptstyle(\nu_{X})_{1}
\scriptstyle\langle s_{\Sigma_{1}(X)},t_{\Sigma_{1}(X)}\rangle
\scriptstyle\langle s_{X},t_{X}\rangle

In the case of call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus, it should be clear that such
a vertical algebra is indeed a model of the rules.

However, in order to ensure that the rules are syntax-directed, we
want to distinguish, for each rule, the head operator of the source of
the conclusion (abstraction for the first rule; application for the
second one). Instead of demanding that
(\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})_{X}
have the form

\Sigma_{1}(X)_{1}\rightarrow X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)
, we thus rather require something of the form

\Sigma_{1}(X)_{1}\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})(0)\times X_{0}(1)
:

{defi}
[Dynamic signatures and vertical
algebras]

•

A
dynamic signature

\Sigma_{1}
consists of

–

a finitary functor
\Sigma_{1}^{F}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}
, and

–

a natural transformation
(\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})_{X}\colon\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})(0)\times X_{0}(1)
.

•

The endofunctor
\check{\Sigma}_{1}

induced
by a dynamic
signature maps any
X
to the composite

\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)\xrightarrow{(\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})_{X}}\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})(0)\times X_{0}(1)\xrightarrow{\nu_{X_{0},0}\times X_{0}(1)}X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)
, where
\nu_{X_{0}}\colon\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})\rightarrow X_{0}
denotes the
\Sigma_{0}
-algebra
structure of
X_{0}
.

•

A
vertical algebra
of a dynamic signature is a vertical
algebra of the induced endofunctor, in the sense of
Definition
3.3
.

Concretely, a vertical algebra is a dashed map making the following
diagram commute.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})(0)\times X_{0}(1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)}
\scriptstyle(\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})_{X}
\scriptstyle\nu_{X_{0},0}\times X_{0}(1)
\scriptstyle\langle s_{X},t_{X}\rangle
{exa}

For call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus, we only need to modify the source
components of the above definition of
\Sigma_{1}
, replacing actual
operations by formal ones, like so:

•

the source of any

is

;

•

the source of any

is

This successfully captures the syntactic transition system:

Proposition 14
.

The initial
\check{\Sigma}_{1}
-algebra
\mathbf{Z}_{\check{\Sigma}_{1}}
, or
\mathbf{Z}
for short,
is an initial vertical algebra, and is isomorphic to the transition
system of Example

.

3.4.
Substitution-closed bisimilarity

There is an obvious notion of bisimulation for transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids:

{defi}

A morphism is
\Sigma_{0}\Trans
is a
functional bisimulation
iff its
underlying morphism in
\mathbf{C}
is.

However, as foreshadowed by Example
3.2
, the relevant
notion in this case combines bisimulation with
substitution-closedness, in the following sense.

{defi}

For any monoid
M
in
\mathbf{C}_{0}
, an
M
-module
is an object
X

equipped with algebra structure
X\otimes M\rightarrow X
for the monad
{-}\otimes M
. A
module morphism is an algebra morphism.

{exa}

The monoid
M
is itself an
M
-module by multiplication, and

M
-modules are closed under limits in
\mathbf{C}_{0}
, so in particular
M^{2}

is an
M
-module, with action given by the composite

M^{2}\otimes M\xrightarrow{\langle\pi_{1}\otimes M,\pi_{2}\otimes M\rangle}(M\otimes M)^{2}\xrightarrow{m_{M}^{2}}M^{2}.

{defi}

For any transition monoid
M
, a span of the form
R\rightarrow M^{2}
in
\mathbf{C}
is

substitution-closed
iff
R_{0}
may be equipped with
M_{0}
-module
structure making the morphism
R_{0}\rightarrow M_{0}^{2}
into an
M_{0}
-module
morphism.

{exa}

To see what this definition has to do with substitution-closedness,
let us observe that if
R
is a relation in
[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
, an element of

(R\otimes M)(n)
is an explicit substitution
r\Lparen\sigma\Rparen
with
r\in R(p)
for
some
p
, and
\sigma\colon p\rightarrow M(n)
. Now, substitution-closedness amounts to
a morphism
m\colon R\otimes M\rightarrow R
commuting with projections, so if
R
is a
relation, then
r
is merely a pair
e\mathrel{R}e^{\prime}
, and the
morphism
m
ensures that
e[\sigma]\mathrel{R}e^{\prime}[\sigma]
.

Proposition 15
.

For any transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid
M
, there is a terminal
substitution-closed bisimulation
\sim_{M}^{\otimes}
, called
substitution-closed
bisimilarity
.

Proof 3.2
.

See Proposition
for a proof in the general case.

Remark 16
.

One may prove that substitution-closed bisimilarity is a relation.

Proposition 17
.

Substitution-closed bisimilarity
\sim_{\mathbf{Z}}^{\otimes}
on the syntactic transition
system
\mathbf{Z}
coincides with applicative bisimilarity.

Proof 3.3
.

Let us denote the open extension of applicative bisimilarity by

\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathit{std}}
, and recall that applicative bisimilarity is denoted by

\sim
. Using Lemma
7
,
\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathit{std}}
is
straightforwardly a substitution-closed bisimulation, so we have

{\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathit{std}}}\subseteq{\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}}}
. But conversely any substitution-closed
bisimulation relation
R
(hence
\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}}
) is in particular a
substitution-closed relation contained in
\sim
on closed terms. It is
thus globally contained in
\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathit{std}}
by
Lemma
7
.

Finally, our main result instantiates to the following.

Theorem 18
.

Substitution-closed bisimilarity is context-closed. More precisely, it
is a transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid, and
{\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}^{2}
is a
transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoid morphism.

In particular, there exists a span morphism
\Sigma_{0}((\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}})_{0})\rightarrow(\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}})_{0}
.

4.
Transition systems and bisimilarity

In this section, we start to abstract over the situation
of §
3
, by introducing a general framework for
transition systems and bisimilarity. In §
4.1
, we first
introduce the ambient setting for this,
pre-Howe contexts
, and
construct a category of transition systems, for any pre-Howe context.
Then, in §
4.2
, we show that transition systems form a
presheaf category. We then exploit this in §
4.3
to
define bisimulation and bisimilarity.

4.1.
Pre-Howe contexts and transition systems

{defi}

A
pre-Howe context
3
3

3

The Howe contexts of
[
BHL
]

may be defined similarly. The difference is that for them,

\mathbf{s}
and
\mathbf{t}
are not necessarily functorial, but

c_{1}\mapsto(\mathbf{s}(c_{1}),\mathbf{t}(c_{1}))
defines a functor

\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\underline{\times}\mathbb{C}_{0}
, where
\mathbb{C}_{0}\underline{\times}\mathbb{C}_{0}
denotes the
category whose objects are pairs of elements of
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, and where a
morphism
(a_{1},a_{2})\rightarrow(b_{1},b_{2})
consists of some indices

i,j\in\{1,2\}
, together with a pair of morphisms
a_{1}\rightarrow b_{i}

and
a_{2}\rightarrow b_{j}
.
consists of

•

a small category
\mathbb{C}_{0}
of
state types
,

•

a small category
\mathbb{C}_{1}
of
transition types
, and

•

two
source
and
target
functors
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

Precomposition by
\mathbf{s}
and
\mathbf{t}
yields functors

\Delta_{\mathbf{s}},\Delta_{\mathbf{t}}\colon\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
mapping any
X\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}

to
X\circ\mathbf{s}
and
X\circ\mathbf{t}
, respectively. Let
\Delta
denote the
pointwise product
\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}\times\Delta_{\mathbf{t}}
.

Intuitively, objects of
\mathbb{C}_{0}
may be thought of as typings (typically
sequents
A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\vdash A
, or merely natural numbers, as
in §
3
), and objects of
\mathbb{C}_{1}
as transition types. The
source and target functors associate to every transition type the
corresponding typings. We now use these functors to define transition
systems.

{defi}

Given any pre-Howe context, a
transition system

X

consists of

•

a
state
presheaf
X_{0}\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
,

•

a
transition
presheaf
X_{1}\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
, and

•

two
source
and
target
natural
transformations
X_{0}\circ\mathbf{s}\leftarrow X_{1}\rightarrow X_{0}\circ\mathbf{t}
, or equivalently a
natural transformation
X_{1}\rightarrow\Delta(X_{0})
.

Proposition 19
.

In any pre-Howe context, transition systems are precisely the objects of
the lax limit category
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta
of the functor

\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\xrightarrow{\Delta}\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
in
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}
, or equivalently the comma
category
\id_{\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}}/\Delta
.

Proof 4.1
.

An object of the lax limit is by construction a triple
(X_{1},X_{0},\partial)
,
where
\partial\colon X_{1}\rightarrow\Delta(X_{0})=X_{0}\mathbf{s}\times X_{0}\mathbf{t}
.

{nota}

In any pre-Howe context, we let
\mathbf{C}:=\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta
, and
denote the projections by

pr_{1}\colon\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
and
pr_{0}\colon\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
, respectively.

Proposition 20
.

The projection functor
-_{0}\colon\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
has a left adjoint mapping any
object
X_{0}
to
\emptyset\rightarrow X_{0}\mathbf{s}\times X_{0}\mathbf{t}
, where
\emptyset
denotes the initial
presheaf on
\mathbb{C}_{1}
. For any
X_{0}
, we call this object the

discrete
transition system on
X_{0}
.

Proof 4.2
.

Straightforward.

{exa}

We can get
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
to be the forgetful functor
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}
by
taking

•

\mathbb{C}_{0}=1
, so that
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}=\widehat{1}\cong\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}
,

•

\mathbb{C}_{1}=1
, so that
\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}
, and

•

\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon 1\rightarrow 1
to be the unique such functor, i.e., the
identity.

A transition system thus consists of sets
V
and
E
together with
a map
E\rightarrow V^{2}
, i.e., a graph.

{exa}

A proof-relevant variant of standard labelled transition
systems (over any set
\mathbb{A}
of labels) may be obtained as follows. We take

•

\mathbb{C}_{0}=1
again,

•

\mathbb{C}_{1}=\mathbb{A}
viewed as a discrete category, and

•

\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
the unique such functor.

Thus, a transition system
X
consists of a set
X_{0}
and sets
X_{a}
for
all
a\in\mathbb{A}
, together with maps
X_{a}\rightarrow X_{0}^{2}
returning the source
and target of each
a
-labelled edge.

More generally, given any graph
\mathbb{L}
, taking
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
to be the
source and target maps
\mathbb{L}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{0}
viewed as functors between discrete
categories, we obtain for
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
a functor equivalent to

\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}/\mathbb{L}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}/\mathbb{L}_{0}
.

{exa}

Let
\mathbb{C}_{0}={\mathbb{F}}^{\mathit{op}}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}=1
, with
\mathbf{s}
and
\mathbf{t}
picking
respectively
0
and
1
. In particular,
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}\cong\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}
. Then,

\Delta(X_{0})=X_{0}(0)\times X_{0}(1)
and we recover the category

\mathbf{C}
of §
3.2
, and its forgetful functor to

\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}=[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
.

4.2.
Transition systems as presheaves

Before introducing bisimulation, let us establish an alternative
characterisation of the category
\mathbf{C}
of transition systems.

Proposition 21
.

The lax limit category
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta
of transition systems is
isomorphic to a presheaf category
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}}
.

Proof 4.3
.

Let
\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}
denote the lax colimit in
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}
of the parallel pair

\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}
. By definition, it is the universal category
with functors and natural transformations as in
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}}
\scriptstyle\mathbf{s}
\scriptstyle\mathbf{t}
\scriptstyle in_{1}
\scriptstyle in_{0}
\scriptstyle s
\scriptstyle t

It thus consists of the coproduct
\mathbb{C}_{1}+\mathbb{C}_{0}
, augmented with arrows

s_{L}\colon\mathbf{s}(L)\rightarrow L
and
t_{L}\colon\mathbf{t}(L)\rightarrow L
for all
L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}
,
naturally in
L
. Presheaves on
\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}
coincide with

\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta
because the presheaf construction turns lax colimits
into lax limits.

{nota}

We often omit the isomorphism
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta\cong\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}}
,
considering it as an implicit coercion. E.g., for any
P\in\mathbb{C}_{0}
,

\mathbf{y}_{P}
may be used to denote the transition system
\underline{P}

with
\underline{P}_{1}=\emptyset
and
\underline{P}_{0}=\mathbf{y}_{P}
.

Similarly,
\mathbf{y}_{L}
may be used to denote the ‘minimal’ transition
system with one transition over
L
, say
\underline{L}
, i.e.,

\underline{L}_{1}=\mathbf{y}_{L}
,

\underline{L}_{0}=\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{t}(L)}
, and the map

\underline{L}_{1}\rightarrow\underline{L}_{0}\mathbf{s}\times\underline{L}_{0}\mathbf{t}
uniquely
determined by the element

(in_{1}(\id_{\mathbf{s}(L)}),in_{2}(\id_{\mathbf{t}(L)}))\in\underline{L}_{0}(\mathbf{s}(L))\times\underline{L}_{0}(\mathbf{t}(L))
.

Finally,
\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{L}
and
\mathbf{y}_{t_{L}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{t}(L)}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{L}

denote the Yoneda embedding of the canonical morphisms
s_{L}
and

t_{L}
from the proof of Proposition
21
.

By Yoneda, we thus have:

Corollary 22
.

For all
X
, we have
\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}_{L},X)\cong X_{1}(L)
and
\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{y}_{P},X)\cong X_{0}(P)
.

{nota}

In the case of call-by-name
\lambda
-calculus, we call
\Downarrow
the unique
object coming from
\mathbb{C}_{1}=1
.

Remark 23
.

Presheaves on
\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}
intuitively have two dimensions,

0
and
1
; the projection functor forgets dimension 1, while the
left adjoint (Proposition
20
) adds an empty
dimension 1, thus lifting its 0-dimensional argument to a
1-dimensional object.

This dimensional intuition leads to the following useful observation
on the forgetful functor.

Proposition 24
.

The forgetful functor
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
preserves all limits and colimits, as
well as image (in the sense of strong epi, mono) factorisations.

Proof 4.4
.

The forgetful functor
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
is equivalent to the
restriction functor
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
, which is
both a left and right adjoint, hence preserves all limits and
colimits. Finally, image factorisations are computed pointwise in
presheaf categories (see, e.g.,
[
Adamek
, §0]
), hence are
preserved by restriction functors.

4.3.
Bisimulation and bisimilarity

Morphisms in
\mathbf{C}
are a generalisation of graph
morphisms, which are a proof-relevant version of functional
simulations. The analogue of functional bisimulations is as follows.

{defi}

A morphism
f\colon X\rightarrow Y
in
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}}
is a
functional
bisimulation
, or a
fibration
, iff it enjoys the (weak)
right lifting property w.r.t.
\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{L}
, for all

L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}
.

Remark 25
.

This definition is strongly inspired by Joyal et al.’s
[
DBLP:conf/lics/JoyalNW93
]
.

Here is a characterisation of fibrations which will be important. Let
us recall that a weak pullback satisfies the same universal property
as a pullback, albeit without uniqueness.

Proposition 26
.

A morphism
f\colon X\rightarrow Y
is a functional bisimulation iff the following
diagram is a pointwise weak pullback.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}\mathbf{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}\mathbf{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}\mathbf{s}}

Remark 27
.

Being a
pointwise
weak pullback means that all squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}(L)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}(L)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}(\mathbf{s}(L))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}(\mathbf{s}(L))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{1})_{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(s_{X})_{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(s_{Y})_{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{0})_{\mathbf{s}(L)}}

should be weak pullbacks, for
L\in\mathbf{o}\mathbf{b}(\mathbb{C}_{1})
. This is weaker than being
a weak pullback.

Proof 4.5

(Proof of Proposition
26
)
.

By Yoneda, a lifting problem in
\mathbf{C}
as below left is the same as a
cone in
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
as below right, and a lifting is the same as a
mediating morphism to
X_{1}
.
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{y}_{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle x
\scriptstyle\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}
\scriptstyle e
\scriptstyle f
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{y}_{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}\mathbf{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}\mathbf{s}}
\scriptstyle x
\scriptstyle e
\scriptstyle f_{1}
\scriptstyle s_{X}
\scriptstyle f_{0}\mathbf{s}
\scriptstyle s_{Y}

(On the left
L
and
\mathbf{s}(L)
are viewed as objects of

\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}}
, hence should technically by written
in_{1}(L)
and

in_{0}(\mathbf{s}(L))
, respectively.)

We now define general bisimulations, based on functional
bisimulations. Usually, one considers bisimulation relations. Here, we
generalise this a bit and consider arbitrary spans:

{defi}

A
simulation
is a span
X\leftarrow R\rightarrow Y
whose left leg is a
fibration. A
bisimulation
is a span of fibrations
(equivalently, a simulation whose converse span is also a
simulation).

A
simulation (resp. bisimulation) relation
is a relation
which is a simulation (resp. bisimulation).

Remark 28
.

Of course, the relevant notion in our applications is
substitution-closed bisimulation, to which we will come below.

Lemma 29
.

Simulation relations and bisimulation relations are stable under unions.

Proof 4.6
.

By symmetry, it is enough to deal with the case of simulation
relations. Consider any family
(R_{i}\hookrightarrow X\times Y)_{i\in I}
of simulation
relations. By Proposition
5
, their union is the
image of their cotupling. But because the domain
\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}
of

\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}
is representable for all
L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}
, any lifting problem

\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\rightarrow\bigcup_{i}R_{i}
lifts to a lifting problem
\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\rightarrow\sum_{i}R_{i}
,
which in turn lifts to a lifting problem
\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\rightarrow R_{i_{0}}
, for
some
i_{0}\in I
. We then find a lifting for the latter because

R_{i_{0}}
is a simulation by hypothesis, which yields a lifting for
the original.

Proposition 30
.

For all
X,Y\in\mathbf{C}
, the full subcategory
\mathbf{B}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{s}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{m}(X,Y)
of spans
between
X
and
Y

which are bisimulations admits a terminal object

\sim_{X,Y}
, called
bisimilarity
.

Proof 4.7
.

As a presheaf category by Proposition
21
,
\mathbf{C}
is
well-powered, so we may consider the union
\sim_{X,Y}
of all
bisimulation relations, which is again a bisimulation by
Lemma
29
. Finally,
\sim_{X,Y}
is terminal, because
any bisimulation
R
factors through its image
im(R)
, which is
again a bisimulation; as a bisimulation relation,
im(R)
thus
embeds into
\sim_{X,Y}
, hence we obtain a morphism

R\twoheadrightarrow im(R)\hookrightarrow{\sim_{X,Y}}
, which is unique by monicity of

{\sim_{X,Y}}\hookrightarrow X\times Y
.

5.
Howe contexts for operational semantics

Operational semantics is a combination of syntax and transition
systems, in the sense that it is about transition systems whose states
form a model of a certain syntax. Our framework for operational
semantics thus combines the frameworks of Fiore et
al.
[
fiore:presheaf
]
for syntax with variable binding, and
of §
4
for transition systems.

In §
5.1
, we introduce the ambient
setting for our framework,
Howe contexts
, which are pre-Howe
contexts equipped with structure modelling substitution. Furthermore,
for any Howe context and pointed strong endofunctor
\Sigma_{0}
on

\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
, we introduce the category
\Sigma_{0}\Trans
of
transition

\Sigma_{0}
-monoids
, which are transition systems whose states form a

\Sigma_{0}
-monoid. We prove that the forgetful functor
\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\mathbf{C}
is
monadic.

In §
5.2
, we then introduce
dynamic signatures
over

\Sigma_{0}
, which specify the dynamics of a transition system. The
(dependent) pair
(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})
then forms what we call an

operational semantics signature
. We then define the models of
any such signature, called
vertical

\Sigma_{1}
-algebras. They form a
category
\Sigma_{1}\algv
, and we prove that the forgetful functor

\Sigma_{1}\algv\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans
is monadic. We also prove that a suitably
constrained construction of the initial
\Sigma_{1}
-algebra is in fact
vertical, yielding an initial vertical
\Sigma_{1}
-algebra. Finally, we
prove that, although both components are monadic, the composite
functor
\Sigma_{1}\algv\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\mathbf{C}
is not.

5.1.
Transition monoid
algebras

In this section, we
introduce Howe contexts, and introduce transition
\Sigma_{0}
-monoids, for
any suitable endofunctor
\Sigma_{0}
.

{defi}

A
Howe context
consists of a pre-Howe context

\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
, together with a monoidal structure on
\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
,
such that the tensor preserves all colimits on the left and filtered

{nota}

As for pre-Howe contexts, we let
\mathbf{C}:=\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta
.

Let us assume that some syntax has been specified by a finitary,

on

.

The category

\scriptstyle\mathscr{U}
\scriptstyle(-)_{0}
\scriptstyle\mathscr{U}_{0}

When

We are now interested in computing initial

-monoids. For this, we

5.2.
Operational semantics signatures

Similarly, we define abstract dynamic signatures, which abstract over
those of Definition
3.3
:

{defi}

Given a Howe context
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
and a pointed strong

\Sigma_{0}\colon\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
, a
dynamic signature

\Sigma_{1}=(\Sigma_{1}^{F},\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})
over
\Sigma_{0}
consists of a finitary functor

\Sigma_{1}^{F}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}
, together with a natural transformation

\Sigma_{1}^{\partial}
with components
\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})\mathbf{s}\times X_{0}\mathbf{t}
.

Let us pack up the static and dynamic notions of signature.

{defi}

An
operational semantics signature

(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})
on a given Howe context

\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
consists of a pointed strong endofunctor
\Sigma_{0}

preserving sifted colimits, together with a dynamic signature
\Sigma_{1}
over
it.

Remark 35
.

Preservation of sifted colimits
[
Sifted
]
is stronger than
finitarity for
\Sigma_{0}
. We need it for
Lemma
below. In a presheaf category like

\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}
, if
\Sigma_{0}
preserves pullbacks (for example, by familiality), it
is equivalent to being finitary and preserving all epis, as seen
from the proof of
[

, Theorem 18.1]
.
In
[

]
, we mistakenly only require

to be finitary, which
yields a gap in the proof of
[
BHL
, Lemma 5.13]
.

{exa}

The endofunctor
\Sigma_{0}(X)(n)=X(n+1)+X(n)^{2}
on
[\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]
preserves
sifted colimits. This easily follows from the fact that sifted colimits
are the ones commuting with products in sets.

Let us now introduce the models of a dynamic signature. We start by
fixing, for the rest of this section, an operational semantics

(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})
on a Howe context
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
.

{defi}

Let

\Sigma_{0}
-monoid

to

where

\Sigma_{0}
-algebra structure of

.

Proposition 36
.

The endofunctor

is finitary and makes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}\Trans}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{0}\mon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\check{\Sigma}_{1}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}}

Proof 5.5
.

Commutativity of the triangle holds by construction, and finitarity

{defi}

A

\check{\Sigma}_{1}\alg$spannedbyallverticalalgebras.\par\begin{thm}The forgetful functor $\Sigma_{1}\algv\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ is monadic, and
furthermore the initial $\check{\Sigma}_{1}$-algebra $\mathbf{Z}_{\check{\Sigma}_{1}}$, or
$\mathbf{Z}$ for short, may be chosen to be vertical, hence is also initial
in $\Sigma_{1}\algv$.
\end{thm}\begin{proof}For the first statement, vertical algebras may be specified as an
equational system, in the sense of~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{FioreHurEquational}{}{}]}, so the
result follows by~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{FioreHurEquational}{}{}, Theorem~6.1]}. For the
second statement, $\mathbf{Z}$ is the colimit of the initial chain
$$\mathbf{Z}_{0}\xrightarrow{!}\check{\Sigma}_{1}(\mathbf{Z}_{0})\xrightarrow{\check{\Sigma}_{1}(!)}\ldots\xrightarrow{\check{\Sigma}_{1}^{n-1}(!)}\check{\Sigma}_{1}^{n}(\mathbf{Z}_{0})\rightarrow\ldots$$(where $\mathbf{Z}_{0}$ is
shorthand for $\mathscr{M}(\mathbf{Z}_{0})$, for readability, which is initial in
$\Sigma_{0}\Trans$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:adj-DM}). The image of this
chain in $\Sigma_{0}\mon$ is the everywhere-identity chain on $\mathbf{Z}_{0}$.
\end{proof}Byconstruction,wehave:\begin{prop}We have $\mathscr{D}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{Z}_{0}$.
\end{prop}\par Letusreadilyannihilateanyhopethatvertical${${}\Sigma$}_1$-algebrasaremonadicover$\mathbf{C}$.\begin{lem}Consider the operational semantics signature of $\lambda$-calculus with
$\Sigma_{0}$ from~\eqref{eq:lambdasyntax} and $\Sigma_{1}$ from
Example~\ref{ex:Sigmaun}. Then, the composite forgetful functor
$\Sigma_{1}\algv\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\mathbf{C}$ is not monadic.
\end{lem}\begin{proof}Let us draw inspiration from the classical example of a
non-monadic composite of monadic
functors~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{BarrWells:ttt}{}{}, p.~107]}, namely the composite
$\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$, where $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}$ denotes the category of
reflexive graphs, and the forgetful functor to sets returns the
set of arrows. One may show that both functors are monadic, but
that their composite is not. By Beck's monadicity
theorem~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{MacLane:cwm}{}{}, Theorem~VI.7.1]}, it suffices to find
a parallel pair $X\rightrightarrows Y$ in $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}$ whose image in sets admits an
absolute coequaliser, and show that this coequaliser is not
created by the composite forgetful functor. The idea is to take
$Y$ to consist of two arrows
\begin{equation*}1\xrightarrow{a}23\xrightarrow{b}4\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}\end{equation*}and $X=1+Y$ to have an additional object, say $0$. We then
define $u,v\colon X\rightarrow Y$ to be the identity on $Y$, and respectively
map $0$ to $2$ and $3$. The coequalisers in $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}$ (top) and
$\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$ (bottom) look as follows, abbreviating each $\id_{C}$ to
just $C$ for readability.

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
\end{center}One easily proves that the one in sets is split, hence absolute.
Because of the composite arrow $b\circ a$ that the
coequaliser in $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{t}$ must have but the one in sets does not, the
coequaliser is not created by the forgetful functor, thus
contradicting monadicity.
\par For proving the lemma, we rely on the $\beta$-rule to mimick
composition in constructing the following parallel pair $X\rightrightarrows Y$
in $\Sigma_{1}\algv$.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$Y$ is the vertical $\Sigma_{1}$-algebra defined as the
$\lambda$-calculus extended with two constants $a$ and $b$, unary
operations $k$ and $l$, and an axiom $b\Downarrow l\Lparen x\Rparen$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$X$ is the vertical $\Sigma_{1}$-algebra extending $Y$ with a constant $c$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@the $\Sigma_{1}$-algebra morphisms $u,v\colon X\rightarrow Y$ respectively map
$c$ to $b$ and $k\Lparen a\Rparen$.
\end{itemize}The coequaliser $E$ of these two morphisms computed in the
presheaf category $\mathbf{C}$ is a quotient of $Y$ by the equation
$b=k\Lparen a\Rparen$. It thus has as reductions $[e]\Downarrow[f]$ between
equivalence classes, for all reductions $e^{\prime}\Downarrow f^{\prime}$ between
representatives $e^{\prime}\in[e]$ and $f^{\prime}\in[f]$. E.g., it has a
reduction $[k\Lparen a\Rparen]\Downarrow[l\Lparen x\Rparen]$, since $b\in[k\Lparen a\Rparen]$ and $b\Downarrow l\Lparen x\Rparen$.
However, $E$ lacks a reduction $[(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a]\Downarrow[l\Lparen x\Rparen]$.
Indeed, $[(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a]$ has a unique representative, namely
$(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a$, whose evaluation in $Y$ gets stuck at $k\Lparen a\Rparen$.
However, the coequaliser in $\Sigma_{1}\algv$ does have such a
reduction by applying the $\beta$-rule:
\begin{equation*}\frac{[\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen]\Downarrow[k\Lparen x\Rparen]\quad[k\Lparen a\Rparen]=[b]\Downarrow[l\Lparen x\Rparen]}{[(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a]\Downarrow[l\Lparen x\Rparen]}~\cdot\end{equation*}Thus, the coequaliser is not created by the forgetful functor.
\par Finally, this coequaliser is split (hence absolute): the
morphism $v\colon X\rightarrow Y$ mapping $c$ to $k\Lparen a\Rparen$ has a section
$f\colon Y\rightarrow X$, which maps $k\Lparen a\Rparen$ to $c$, and the coequaliser arrow
$e\colon Y\rightarrow E$ has a section $g\colon E\rightarrow Y$ mapping $k\Lparen a\Rparen$ to $b$. It
is straightforward to check that this indeed defines a split
coequaliser, i.e., that $g\circ e=u\circ f$.
\end{proof}\begin{rem}A crucial point is that $g$ may (and does) map $a$ and $k$ to
themselves (the latter being necessary to preserve the target of
$(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\Downarrow k\Lparen x\Rparen$), and $k\Lparen a\Rparen$ to $b\neq k\Lparen a\Rparen$. Indeed, $g$ lives
in $\mathbf{C}$, as opposed to $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$, hence need not preserve
substitution. All that is required is naturality. But $k\Lparen a\Rparen$,
being closed, cannot be the target of any transition, and by
induction cannot be the source of any transition either, hence
the result.
\par Also, let us stress that in $Y$, $(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a$ does not
evaluate, since $k\Lparen a\Rparen$ itself does not. Similarly, in $E$, which
is not saturated by the evaluation rules, we do have the
premises $(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\Downarrow k\Lparen x\Rparen$ and $k\Lparen a\Rparen=b\Downarrow l\Lparen x\Rparen$, but not the
conclusion $(\lambda x.k\Lparen x\Rparen)\ a\Downarrow l\Lparen x\Rparen$.
\end{rem}\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Substitution-closed bisimilarity}
We have now introduced our notion of syntactic transition system,
given by $\Sigma_{0}$-transition monoids in a Howe context, and explained how
to generate such systems from operational semantics signatures. In
this section, we incorporate substitution into the notions of
bisimulation and bisimilarity introduced in~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:bisimex}, which
yields substitution-closed bisimilarity. We then state our main
theorem, for which we include a high-level proof sketch.
\par In order to introduce substitution-closed bisimilarity, we first lift
the notion of bisimulation to $\Sigma_{0}$-monoids,
generalising~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:substclosed:ex}:
\defi
A morphism in $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ is a \emph{functional bisimulation} iff its
underlying morphism in $\mathbf{C}$ is. A span is a \emph{simulation} iff its
left leg is a functional bisimulation, and a \emph{bisimulation} iff
both of its legs are functional bisimulations.
Let us readily prove the following characterisation by lifting,
recalling from Notation~\ref{not:L} that $\mathscr{L}\colon\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ is left
adjoint to the forgetful functor.
\begin{prop}A morphism in $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ is a functional bisimulation
iff it has the right lifting property w.r.t.\ $\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}})\colon\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)})\rightarrow\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{L})$, for all $L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}$.
\end{prop}\begin{proof}By adjunction.
\end{proof}\par As seen in Example~\ref{ex:bisimZ}, we now want to go beyond
bisimilarity, and introduce abstract versions of substitution-closed
bisimulation and bisimilarity. For this, let us give the general
definition of modules over a monoid.
\par\defi For any monoid $M$ in a monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$, let $M\Mod$ denote
the category of algebras for the monad ${-}\otimes M$.
An $M$-module thus consists of an object $X$ equipped with an action
$X\otimes M\rightarrow X$ of $M$ satisfying straightforward coherence conditions.
\par\exa$M$ itself is an $M$-module, with action given by multiplication.
\par Before going into substitution-closed bisimulation, let us record the
following useful properties of modules in a Howe context.
\begin{prop}In any Howe context, for all monoids $M$ in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$,
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@the forgetful functor $M\Mod\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$ creates all limits
and colimits, and furthermore
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@the category $M\Mod$ is regular and the forgetful functor
$M\Mod\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$
creates image factorisations.
\end{itemize}\end{prop}\begin{proof}For creation of limits and colimits:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@As algebras for the monad ${-}\otimes M$, $M$-modules are closed
under limits.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@They are also closed under all types of colimits
preserved by ${-}\otimes M$, i.e., all of them by definition of Howe
contexts.
\end{itemize}Thus, $M\Mod$ is complete and cocomplete, hence regularity reduces to
showing that the pullback of any regular epi is again a regular
epi. So let us consider any pullback square

$f$ is a regular epi there too. So by regularity of the presheaf
category $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$, $v$ is a regular epi in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$. Equivalently, it is a
coequaliser of its kernel pair. But by creation of limits the kernel
pair uniquely lifts to a kernel pair in $M\Mod$, and by creation of
colimits $v$ is a coequaliser there too. This shows that $M\Mod$ is
regular.
\par Finally, given $X,Z\in M\Mod$, let us consider any image

morphism $f\colon X\rightarrow Z$ in $M\Mod$, i.e., $e$ is a regular epi and $m$
is a mono in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$. In this situation, $e$ is the coequaliser of its
kernel pair in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$, but, as we just saw, this kernel pair lifts to
a kernel pair in $M\Mod$, whose coequaliser is created by the
forgetful functor, hence $e$ is a coequaliser, hence a regular epi
in $M\Mod$. Finally, $f$ also coequalises the kernel pair, hence the
existence of a unique mediating morphism $Y\rightarrow Z$ in $M\Mod$, which
must be $m$ by faithfulness of the forgetful functor $M\Mod\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$. Thus, $m$ is also a morphism in $M\Mod$. Finally, its monicity
follows again by faithfulness of the forgetful functor.
\end{proof}\par Let us now introduce substitution-closed spans, first in an arbitrary
monoidal category, and then in a Howe context. This then leads us to
substitution-closed bisimulation.
\defi
In a monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$ with binary products, given a monoid $M$
and $M$-modules $X$ and $Y$, a \emph{substitution-closed} span is a
span $p\colon R\rightarrow X\times Y$ equipped with $M$-module structure $\rho\colon R\otimes M\rightarrow R$ on
$R$, such that $p\colon R\rightarrow X\times Y$ is an $M$-module morphism.
The last condition is equivalent to commutation of the following
diagram.

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
\end{center}\defi Consider any Howe context $\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}$ and
transition monoid $M\in\mathbf{C}$. Let $X,Y\in\mathbf{C}$ be equipped with $M_{0}$-module structure
on $X_{0}$ and $Y_{0}$. A \emph{substitution-closed} span is a span
$R\rightarrow X\times Y$ equipped with substitution-closed structure on
$R_{0}\rightarrow X_{0}\times Y_{0}$.
\par\defi For any Howe context $\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}$ and transition monoid $M\in\mathbf{C}$, a \emph{substitution-closed simulation (resp.\ bisimulation)} is a substitution-closed span $R\rightarrow M^{2}$ (viewing
$M_{0}$ itself as an $M_{0}$-module by Example~\ref{ex:MasanMmodule})
which is a simulation (resp.\ bisimulation).
Let $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{s}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{m}^{\otimes}(M)$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathbf{C}/M^{2}$ spanned by
substitution-closed bisimulations.
Let us now prove the existence of substitution-closed bisimilarity.
\begin{lem}Substitution-closed simulation and bisimulation relations are stable
under unions.
\end{lem}\begin{proof}By Lemma~\ref{lem:bisimunion}, the union of a family of
substitution-closed simulation (resp.\ bisimulation) relations is
again a simulation (resp.\ bisimulation) relation. But by
Proposition~\ref{prop:modulespreserve}, the union in $\mathbf{C}$ is again
substitution-closed, which concludes the proof.
\end{proof}\begin{prop}For any Howe context $\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}$ and monoid
$M\in\mathbf{C}$, the category $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{s}\mathbf{i}\mathbf{m}^{\otimes}(M)$ of
substitution-closed bisimulations over $M$ admits a terminal object
$\sim^{\otimes}_{M}$, called \emph{substitution-closed bisimilarity}.
\end{prop}\begin{proof}Straightforward generalisation of the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:bisim} using the lemma.
\end{proof}\par\nota When $M=\mathbf{Z}$, we abbreviate $\sim^{\otimes}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ to just $\sim^{\otimes}$.
\par We now want to state the abstract version of our main theorem, but we
need an additional hypothesis, which we now introduce. The idea is
essentially that $\Sigma_{1}$ should preserve functional bisimulations, which
does not quite make sense, because the codomain of $\Sigma_{1}^{F}$ is
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}$, where no notion of functional bisimulation has been
defined yet. Recalling Proposition~\ref{prop:sim:wpbk}, we work
around this as follows.
\defi
A dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1}=(\Sigma_{1}^{F},\Sigma_{1}^{\partial})$ \emph{preserves functional
bisimulations} iff for any functional bisimulation $f\colon R\rightarrow X$ in
$\Sigma_{0}\Trans$, the following square is a pointwise weak pullback.
