\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{equation}\par\begin{rem}It may not be obvious that the dynamic signature for call-by-name
$\lambda$-calculus preserves functional bisimulations. We will come back
to this in~\lx@sectionsign\ref{s:cellularity} by showing that it satisfies a
sufficient condition, cellularity.
\end{rem}\par\begin{rem}It may seem linguistically inappropriate to say that $\Sigma_{1}$ preserves
functional bisimulations, since $\Sigma_{1}$ is not merely a functor, and we
have not even defined fibrations in the codomain category $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}$
anyway. We will justify the terminology in
Proposition~\ref{prop:ling-mischief}, but for now let us move on
directly to the main result.
\end{rem}\par\begin{thm}If $\Sigma_{1}$ preserves functional bisimulations, then substitution-closed
bisimilarity is context-closed. More precisely, ${\sim^{\otimes}}$ is a
transition {$\Sigma_{0}$}-monoid, and ${\sim^{\otimes}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ is a
transition {$\Sigma_{0}$}-monoid morphism.
\end{thm}\par\begin{proof}The proof takes inspiration from Howe's original method.
\begin{enumeratewide}\enumerate@item@We first define the \emph{Howe closure} $H_{0}$
of substitution-closed bisimilarity $\sim_{0}^{\otimes}$ on states as the initial
$\Sigma_{0}^{H}$-monoid for the pointed strong endofunctor $\Sigma_{0}^{H}$ on
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}/\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ defined by $\Sigma_{0}^{H}(R)=\Sigma_{0}(R)+(R;{\sim_{0}^{\otimes}})$. We then
show that, by construction, $H_{0}$ is a $\Sigma_{0}$-monoid and both
projections are $\Sigma_{0}$-monoid morphisms. \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\par\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@We then define the \emph{transition Howe closure} ${H}$ of (the
full) substitution-closed bisimilarity ${\sim^{\otimes}}$, as an initial algebra for
an endofunctor $\Sigma_{1}^{H}$ on a suitable category $\mathbf{C}^{H}_{\mathbf{Z}}$. Very roughly,
$\mathbf{C}^{H}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the category of spans $R\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ whose projection is
precisely $H_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}^{2}_{0}$, and $\Sigma_{1}^{H}(R)=\check{\Sigma}_{1}(R)+(R;{\sim^{\otimes}})$. We
show:
\begin{lem}There exists a span morphism $\mathbf{i}^{H}\colon{\sim^{\otimes}}\rightarrow H$.
\end{lem}\par\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@Next comes the key lemma:
\begin{lem}If $\Sigma_{1}$ preserves functional bisimulations, then the transition
Howe closure ${H}$ is a substitution-closed simulation.
\end{lem}\par\begin{rem}Since ${H_{0}}$ is a $\Sigma_{0}$-monoid by construction, $H$ is
easily seen to be substitution-closed, so the lemma really is
about it being a simulation.
\end{rem}The key lemma is proved by characterising $H$ as an initial algebra
for a different endofunctor on a different category, whose initial
chain involves iterated applications of $\Sigma_{1}$ (preserving simulations by
hypothesis) to $\pi_{1}\colon\mathscr{M}(H_{0})\rightarrow\mathscr{M}(\mathbf{Z}_{0})$, which is trivially a simulation.
\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\par\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@In the standard proof method, the next step is
to prove that the transitive closure of $H_{0}$ is symmetric. But in
our case $H_{0}$ is a general span, not a relation. In order to avoid
some coherence issues, we introduce a suitable notion of
\emph{relational} transitive closure for general spans, denoted by
$-^{\overline{+}}$, which is equipped with a canonical
map $\mathbf{i}^{\overline{+}}_{R}\colon R\rightarrow R^{\overline{+}}$ for each span $R$. We then show:
\par\begin{lem}The relational transitive closure ${H_{0}}{}^{\overline{+}}$ of the
Howe closure $H_{0}$ on states is symmetric.
\end{lem}\par As substitution-closed simulations are closed under transitive
closure, we obtain
\begin{cor}${H}{}^{\overline{+}}$ is a substitution-closed simulation which
is symmetric on states.
\end{cor}\par We then use the following lemma (proved in~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:sym-tran-clos}).
\begin{lem}For any substitution-closed simulation $R$ such that $R_{0}$ is
symmetric, there exists a substitution-closed bisimulation $R^{\prime}$
and a span morphism $\mathbf{i}^{\prime}_{R}\colon R\rightarrow R^{\prime}$.
\end{lem}\par By terminality of $\sim^{\otimes}$, we thus get a unique morphism
${!}_{{{H}{}^{\overline{+}}}{}^{\prime}}\colon{{{H}{}^{\overline{+}}}{}^{\prime}}\rightarrow{\sim^{\otimes}}$ over $\mathbf{Z}^{2}$.
\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\par\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@From the chain \hfil$${\sim^{\otimes}}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{i}^{H}}{H}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{i}^{\overline{+}}_{H}}{{H}{}^{\overline{+}}}\xrightarrow{\mathbf{i}^{\prime}_{R}}{{H}{}^{\overline{+}}}{}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{{!}_{{{H}{}^{\overline{+}}}{}^{\prime}}}{\sim^{\otimes}}$$we get by terminality that ${\sim^{\otimes}}$ is a retract of a
transition {$\Sigma_{0}$}-monoid, namely ${H}$. The result then readily
follows from monadicity of transition {$\Sigma_{0}$}-monoids
(Proposition~\ref{prop:SigmaMon-monadic}) and the following result,
taking $X={H}$, $Y={\sim^{\otimes}}$, and $Z=\mathbf{Z}^{2}$.\end{enumeratewide}\end{proof}\par\begin{lem}Consider a monad $T\colon\mathscr{C}\rightarrow\mathscr{C}$ on any category $\mathscr{C}$, $T$-algebras $X$
and $Z$, and morphisms $X\mathrel{\hbox to14.56pt{\vbox to10.48pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\;\lower-2.59998pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{}{}{}{{{}{}}}{{}}{}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 10.52 0}{fill:none} {{}{{}}{}{}{{}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{5.32004pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -2.88 3.32 C -2.35 1.33 -1.18 0.39 0 0 C -1.18 -0.39 -2.35 -1.33 -2.88 -3.32}{fill:none} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{7.80002pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -2.88 3.32 C -2.35 1.33 -1.18 0.39 0 0 C -1.18 -0.39 -2.35 -1.33 -2.88 -3.32}{fill:none} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}Z$ in $\mathscr{C}$ such
that the composite is a $T$-algebra morphism, $e$ is a split epi,
and $m$ is monic. Then there is a unique $T$-algebra structure on
$Y$ such that $e$ and $m$ both are $T$-algebra morphisms.
\end{lem}\begin{proof}Let $s\colon Y\rightarrow X$ denote any section of $e$.
The desired structure is given by

\end{proof}\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Preservation of functional bisimulations, and cellularity}
Let us now consider the main hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:main},
preservation of functional bisimulations. In~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:rephrase}, we
rephrase the condition in a way that makes more sense linguistically,
i.e., by an actual preservation condition. We then work towards a
characterisation in terms of cellularity. In~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:fam}, we first
briefly recall \emph{familial}
functors~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Diers1978Spectres,DBLP:journals/mscs/CarboniJ95,Weber:famfun}{}{}]},
and show that the operational semantics signature for call-by-name
$\lambda$-calculus gives rise to two familial functors, in a suitable sense.
In~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:cell}, we restrict attention to the case where both
components of the dynamic signature give rise to familial functors in
this sense, and show that preservation of functional bisimulations is
then equivalent to a \emph{cellularity}
condition~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{garner:hal-01246365,BHL}{}{}]}, which itself comes with a
useful sufficient condition.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{An alternative characterisation}

\end{prop}\begin{proof}Finitarity holds because it does pointwise, by assumption. The
diagram commutes by construction.
\end{proof}\par\par In $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ (or, through the isomorphism of
Proposition~\ref{prop:Csource}, in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$), we may
define functional bisimulations by analogy with
Definition~\ref{def:fib}.
\defi
A morphism $f\colon X\rightarrow Y$ in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ is a \emph{functional
bisimulation}, or a \emph{fibration}, iff it enjoys the (weak)
right lifting property w.r.t.\ $\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}\colon\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{s}(L)}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{L}$, for all
$L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}$.
\par\begin{prop}A dynamic signature preserves functional bisimulations
(Definition~\ref{def:Sigma1-preserve-bisim}) iff the
induced functor $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$ does.
\end{prop}\begin{proof}The functor $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ maps any functional bisimulation
$f\colon R\rightarrow Y$ to the square~\eqref{eq:presfib}, and just as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:sim:wpbk} a morphism in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ is
a functional bisimulation iff the corresponding square in
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}$ is a pointwise weak pullback.
\end{proof}\par\par\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Familiality}
In the previous sections, we have seen that functional bisimulations
may be defined by lifting both in $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ and $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$. We
now want to exploit this to obtain a characterisation of preservation
of functional bisimulations, which will then lead us to useful
sufficient conditions.
\par For this, let us briefly recall familial functors, and show that the
functors $\Sigma_{0}$ and $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$ induced
by the dynamic signature for call-by-name $\lambda$-calculus are familial.
\par Familial functors are a generalisation of polynomial functors on
sets, i.e., functors of the form $F(X)=\sum_{o\in O}X^{n_{o}}$, where $O$
is a set of `operations', and $n_{o}\in\mathbb{N}$ is the `arity' of any $o\in O$.
We want to generalise this to presheaf categories.
\exa
Consider for
example the `free category' monad $T$ on $\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}$. Analysing and
abstracting over the definition of $T$, we will arrive at the notion
of familial functor. Let us first recall that graphs are presheaves
over the category

\end{center}$T$ does not change the vertex set, and an edge of $T(G)$ is
merely a path in $G$. Indexing this by the length of the path, we
obtain
\begin{center}$T(G)[0]\cong\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{y}_{[0]},G)$ \hfil and \hfil$T(G)[1]\cong\sum_{n}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}([n],G)$,
\end{center}where $[n]$ denotes the filiform graph $\bullet\rightarrow\bullet\ldots\rightarrow\bullet$ with $n$ edges
(which is consistent with $[0]$ and $[1]$ through the Yoneda
embedding). Furthermore, the source of a path $[n]\rightarrow G$
is obtained as the composite
$$[0]\xrightarrow{s_{n}}[n]\rightarrow G\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$where the first morphism selects the first vertex of the path.
Similarly the target is obtained by precomposition with the
morphism, say $t_{n}$, selecting the last vertex.
\par From these observations, let us now explain how the whole of $T$
may be derived from
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@the graph $T(1)$, which generalises the set of operations, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a functor $\el(T(1))\rightarrow\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}$, morally describing the arity of
each operation,
\end{itemize}where we recall from MacLane and Moerdijk~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{MM}{}{}]}:
\defi
The \emph{category of elements} $\el(X)$ of a presheaf $X$ over any
category $\mathbb{C}$ has pairs $(c,x)$ with $x\in X(c)$ as objects, and a
morphism $f\upharpoonright x^{\prime}\colon(c,x)\rightarrow(c^{\prime},x^{\prime})$ for all $f\colon c\rightarrow c^{\prime}$ such that
$X(f)(x^{\prime})=x$.
The graph $T(1)$ has a single vertex, and as many paths as we can derive from
a single endo-edge on this vertex: $\mathbb{N}$, because there is one for each length.
The category of elements of $T(1)$ thus looks like the following,

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
\end{center}The promised expression of $T$ in terms of $T(1)$ and $E$ is:
$$T(G)(c)\cong\sum_{o\in T(1)(c)}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{p}\mathbf{h}(E(c,o),G).$$\par\defi A functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ to some presheaf category is \emph{familial}
iff we have a natural isomorphism
$$F(X)(c)\cong\sum_{o\in O(c)}\mathscr{A}(E(c,o),X)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$for some presheaf $O\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ and functor $E\colon\el(O)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}$. The
presheaf $O$ is called the presheaf of \emph{operations}, or the
\emph{spectrum}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Diers1978Spectres}{}{}]} of $F$, while $E$ is
called the \emph{arity}, or \emph{exponent} functor.
\begin{rem}This definition is a bit elliptic, so let us make functoriality
more explicit.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@Functoriality in $X$ is by post-composition.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For functoriality in $c$, for any $f\colon c\rightarrow d$ in $\mathbb{C}$
and $o\in O(d)$, letting $o^{\prime}=o\cdot f$, we get a morphism
$f\upharpoonright o\colon(c,o^{\prime})\rightarrow(d,o)$ in $\el(O)$, hence a morphism
$E(f\upharpoonright o)\colon E(c,o^{\prime})\rightarrow E(d,o)$. Precomposition by this morphisms
yields a map $$\mathscr{A}(E(d,o),X)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}(E(c,o^{\prime}),X).$$Postcomposing with
the obvious coproduct injections, and cotupling, we get the desired map
$$\sum_{o\in O(d)}\mathscr{A}(E(d,o),X)\rightarrow\sum_{o^{\prime}\in O(c)}\mathscr{A}(E(c,o^{\prime}),X).$$\end{itemize}\end{rem}\begin{rem}If $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object, we always have $O\cong F(1)$.
\end{rem}\par\exa Let us show that the endofunctor $\Sigma_{0}\colon\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$
from~\lx@sectionsign\ref{s:exsyntax} for $\lambda$-calculus is familial, where we
recall that $\mathbb{C}_{0}={\mathbb{F}}^{\mathit{op}}$. Indeed, we then have
$$\begin{array}[t]{rcll}\Sigma_{0}(X)(n)&=&X(n+1)+X(n)^{2}\\
&\cong&\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}(\mathbf{y}_{n+1},X)+\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}(2\cdot\mathbf{y}_{n},X)\\
\end{array}$$Thus, we choose:
\begin{center}$\begin{array}[t]{rcl}O(n)&=&\{\mathrm{abs},\mathrm{app}\}\end{array}$
\hfil$\begin{array}[t]{rcl}E(n,\mathrm{abs})&=&\mathbf{y}_{n+1}\\
E(n,\mathrm{app})&=&2\cdot\mathbf{y}_{n}\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}\end{array}$
\end{center}These definitions can be straightforwardly upgraded to functors
$O\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$ and $E\colon\el(O)\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$, and we get the desired
isomorphism.
\par\exa Let us now show that the functor
$\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$ for call-by-name
$\lambda$-calculus is familial. By definition, it maps any $X$ to the
set-map $X_{0}(1)+A_{\beta}(X)\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}(X_{0})(0)$ defined in
Example~\ref{ex:Sigmaun}. Let us transfer this across the
isomorphism $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}\cong\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ (recalling
Remark~\ref{rk:Csigma}), and show that $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ may be
expressed as in Definition~\ref{def:familial}, first for
$c\in\mathbb{F}$ and then for $c=\Downarrow$.
\par For $c=n\in\mathbb{F}$, we almost may proceed as for $\Sigma_{0}$, except that the
domain category has changed (from $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$ to $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$). But

&\cong&\Sigma_{0}\Trans(\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{n+1}),X)+\Sigma_{0}\Trans(\mathscr{L}(2\cdot\mathbf{y}_{n}),X)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}\end{array}$$so we may (partially) define

\par We have thus defined the actions of the functors
$O\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ and $E\colon\el(O)\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans$ on objects. On
morphisms, the only non-obvious point is the image of
$s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright\lambda\text{-}\mathrm{val}$ and $s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright\beta\text{-}\mathrm{red}$.
The former morphism is mapped to the identity on
$E(0,\mathrm{abs})=\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{1})=E(\Downarrow,\lambda\text{-}\mathrm{val})$.
The latter is mapped to the composite
\begin{equation}\mathscr{L}(2\cdot\mathbf{y}_{0})\xrightarrow{\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{s_{\Downarrow}}+\mathbf{y}_{0})}\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{\Downarrow}+\mathbf{y}_{0})\xrightarrow{in_{2}}E_{\beta}\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}\end{equation}This achieves the desired isomorphism
$\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}(X)(c)\cong\sum_{o\in O(c)}\Sigma_{0}\Trans(E(c,o),X)$.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Cellularity}
We now want to exploit familiality to obtain an alternative
characterisation of preservation of functional bisimulations. The
starting point is the observation that when a functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is
familial, say as $F(A)(c)=\sum_{o\in O(c)}\mathscr{A}(E(c,o),A)$, then any
morphism of the form $f\colon\mathbf{y}_{c}\rightarrow F(A)$, corresponding by Yoneda and
familiality to some pair $(o,\phi)$ with $\phi\colon E(c,o)\rightarrow A$, factors as
$$\mathbf{y}_{c}\xrightarrow{(o,\id_{E(c,o)})}F(E(c,o))\xrightarrow{F(\phi)}F(A)\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}$$Furthermore, the first component $(o,\id_{E(c,o)})$ is easily seen to
be \emph{generic}, in the following sense.
\par\defi Given any functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\mathscr{B}$, a morphism $\xi\colon B\rightarrow F(A)$ is
\emph{$F$-generic} (or \emph{generic} for short) whenever
for all $\chi$, $f$, and $g$ making the square below (solid) commute,

\lxSVG@closescope {{

\end{center}there is a unique lifting $k$ (dashed) such that $F(k)\circ\xi=\chi$ and
$g\circ k=f$.
\par In fact, we have the following important alternative characterisation
of familial functors to presheaf categories.
\begin{thm}For any functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ such that $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal
object, $F$ is familial iff all morphisms $f\colon X\rightarrow F(A)$ factor as
$$X\xrightarrow{\xi}F(U)\xrightarrow{F(\phi)}F(A)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$with $\xi$ generic.
\end{thm}\begin{proof}This is~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{garner:hal-01246365}{}{}, Proposition~3.8]}, using the
remark just before it.
\end{proof}\begin{rem}The factorisation is essentially unique.
\end{rem}\par The characterisation of familiality in terms of generic morphisms
allows us to characterise familial functors which preserve fibrations,
as cellular functors, which we now introduce.
\par\par\defi A \emph{category with generating cofibrations} is a category
$\mathscr{C}$ equipped with a set $\mathbb{J}$ of morphisms.
\par For any such $(\mathscr{C},\mathbb{J})$, as in~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:notation}, we call
\emph{fibrations} all morphisms in ${\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork}$, and
\emph{cofibrations} all morphisms in ${{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}}$.
\par\exa In $\Sigma_{0}\Trans$, with generating cofibrations consisting of all
morphisms $\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}})$, fibrations are precisely functional
bisimulations, by Proposition~\ref{prop:bisimadj}.
\par\exa In $\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$, with generating cofibrations consisting of all
morphisms $\mathbf{y}_{s_{L}}$, fibrations are precisely functional
bisimulations, by Definition~\ref{def:fbisim:Csource}.
\par\defi For any categories with generating cofibrations $(\mathscr{A},\mathbb{J})$ and
$(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{K})$, such that $\mathbb{C}$ is small and $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object, a familial functor
$F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is \emph{cellular} iff for all commuting squares

\par Before exploiting cellularity as promised, let us briefly pause to
give an equivalent characterisation of cellularity in suitably nice
cases.
\par\defi Let us consider any familial functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, say as
$F(A)(c)=\sum_{o\in O(c)}\mathscr{A}(E(c,o),A)$, such that $\mathbb{C}$ is small and $\mathscr{A}$
has a terminal object. Then, for any operation $o\in F(1)(d)$ and
morphism $s\colon c\rightarrow d$ in $\mathbb{C}$, the \emph{$s$-arity} of $o$, or its
\emph{boundary arity} when $s$ is clear from context, is the
morphism $E(d,o\upharpoonright s)\colon E(c,o\cdot s)\rightarrow E(d,o)$ in $\mathscr{A}$.
\par\par\nota Let $\chi_{o}$ denote the generic morphism $\mathbf{y}_{d}\rightarrow F(E(d,o))$
induced by any operation $o\in F(1)(d)$.

a generating cofibration (i.e., is in $\mathbb{K}$), then the diagram

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
\end{center}is of the form~\eqref{eq:gensquare} by construction. We thus have
by definition:
\begin{prop}Let us consider any cellular $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ between categories with
generating cofibrations $(\mathscr{A},\mathbb{J})$ and $(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{K})$ such that $\mathbb{C}$ is
small and $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object. Then, for any representable
morphism $\mathbf{y}_{s}\colon\mathbf{y}_{c}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{d}$ in $\mathbb{K}$, the $s$-arity of any operation
$o\in F(1)(d)$ is a cofibration.
\end{prop}\par When all domains and codomains of generating cofibrations $k\in\mathbb{K}$
are representable, say as $\mathbf{y}_{s}\colon\mathbf{y}_{c}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}_{d}$, then all generic
morphisms $\chi\colon D\rightarrow F(Y)$, with $D$ a codomain of some generating
cofibration, are isomorphic to some $\mathbf{y}_{d}\rightarrow F(E(d,o))$, for some
operation $o\in F(1)(d)$, and the morphism $\delta$ must then be
isomorphic to $E(d,o\upharpoonright s)\colon E(c,o\cdot s)\rightarrow E(d,o)$. We thus get a partial
converse to Proposition~\ref{prop:karities}:
\begin{prop}For any categories with generating cofibrations $(\mathscr{A},\mathbb{J})$ and
$(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{K})$, such that $\mathbb{C}$ is small, $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object, and
all domains and codomains of generating cofibrations $k\in\mathbb{K}$ are
representable, a familial functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is cellular iff the
boundary arities of all operations are cofibrations.
\end{prop}\par Returning to the general case, let us now prove a first
characterisation of preservation of fibrations in terms of
cellularity.
\begin{lem}For any categories with generating cofibrations $(\mathscr{A},\mathbb{J})$ and
$(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{K})$ such that $\mathbb{C}$ is small and $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object, a
familial functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ preserves fibrations iff it is
cellular.
\end{lem}\par\begin{proof}Let us first prove the `if' direction. We must show that for any

\end{proof}\par\begin{cor}For any categories with generating cofibrations $(\mathscr{A},\mathbb{J})$ and
$(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{K})$, such that $\mathbb{C}$ is small, $\mathscr{A}$ has a terminal object, and
all domains and codomains of generating cofibrations $k\in\mathbb{K}$ are
representable, a familial functor $F\colon\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ preserves fibrations
iff the boundary arities of all operations are cofibrations.
\par\end{cor}\begin{proof}By Proposition~\ref{prop:cellular:boundaries} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:characfib}.
\end{proof}\par Here is the announced characterisation of preservation of functional
bisimulations, which follows directly from Lemma~\ref{lem:characfib}
and Corollary~\ref{cor:characfib2}.
\begin{cor}In any Howe context, for any operational semantics signature
$(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})$, let $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ be familial
with exponent $E\colon\el(\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}(1))\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}\Trans$. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerati}\enumerate@item@$\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ preserves functional bisimulations;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@$\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ is cellular;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@the boundary arities of all operations
are cofibrations, i.e., for all $L\in\mathbb{C}_{1}$ and
$o\in\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}(1)(L)$, the morphism
$$E(s_{L}\upharpoonright o)\colon E(\mathbf{s}(L),o\cdot s_{L})\rightarrow E(L,o)$$is a cofibration.
\end{enumerati}\end{cor}\par This characterisation of preservation of functional bisimulations in
terms of cofibrations is easier to prove in practice, since
cofibrations in turn admit the following well-known characterisation.

\end{center}\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@A \emph{relative $\mathbb{J}$-cell
complex} is a (potentially transfinite) composite of basic relative $\mathbb{J}$-cell complexes.
\end{itemize}\par\propC[{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Hovey}{}{}, Lemma~2.1.10]}}]
For any set $\mathbb{J}$ of maps in a locally presentable category, all
relative $\mathbb{J}$-cell complexes are cofibrations in the generated
weak factorisation system $({{}^{\pitchfork}{({\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})}},{\mathbb{J}}^{\pitchfork})$.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Applications}
In this section, we apply our results to show that substitution-closed
bisimilarity is a congruence in concrete examples.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Call-by-name}
We have already specified the syntax (\lx@sectionsign\ref{s:exsyntax}) and
transitions (\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:opsem}) of call-by-name $\lambda$-calculus. We have
also seen (Example~\ref{ex:cbn:familial}) that the induced functor
$\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$ is familial. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{cor:cellularenough}, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:cellscof}, congruence of substitution-closed
bisimilarity will follow if we prove that the boundary arities
$E(s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright o)$ corresponding to both transition rules are relative cell
complexes.
\par The boundary arity $E(s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright\lambda\text{-}\mathrm{val})$ is an identity,
hence trivially a relative cell complex.
\par For the $\beta$-rule, it is not entirely trivial that the
boundary arity
$E(s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright\beta\text{-}\mathrm{red})$ of the second
transition rule, defined as the composite~\eqref{eq:Ebetasource}, is a
cofibration. But, as (essentially) noted in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{BHL}{}{}, Example~5.21]},
it is a relative cell complex by construction, as both components are
pushouts of $\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{s_{\Downarrow}})$, as should be clear from the following
diagram, where again $\bar{\chi}$ is as in Definition~\ref{def:chibar}.

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
\end{center}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Call-by-value}
Let us now treat the call-by-value variant of untyped $\lambda$-calculus,
essentially as in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{OngApplicative,Pitts:howe}{}{}]}. In this setting,
it is important to distinguish substitution by values and by
terms. Indeed, letting $I$ denote the identity $\lambda x.x$, the terms
$e=\lambda x.I$ and $e^{\prime}=\lambda x.((\lambda y.I)\ x)$ are contextually equivalent,
since during evaluation in any context, the bound variable $x$ will only
be replaced with a value. However, if one defines applicative
bisimulation naively, i.e., requiring it to be closed under arbitrary
substitution, then $e$ and $e^{\prime}$ are not bisimilar, as $I$ is not
bisimilar to $(\lambda y.I)\ \Omega$ -- which diverges. We thus want to restrict
to value substitution -- which our treatment in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{BHL}{}{}]} overlooks!
\par Here is one way of doing this. The idea is to have two sorts, one for
values and the other for general terms. We thus would like
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$ to be equivalent to the category $[\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}]_{f}$
of finitary endofunctors on $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}$. But
$$[\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}]_{f}\simeq[2\cdot\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}_{f}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]\simeq[2\cdot\mathbb{F}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}],$$so we take $\mathbb{C}_{0}$ to be the opposite of $2\cdot\mathbb{F}^{2}$. By the
equivalence, composition of finitary endofunctors equips
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$ with monoidal structure, and we denote the two sorts by
$\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, respectively for ``programs'' and ``values''. In the
presheaf point of view, we denote by $(m,n)_{\mathbf{p}}$ and $(m,n)_{\mathbf{v}}$,
respectively, objects in the first and second term of
$2\times\mathbb{F}^{2}=\mathbb{F}^{2}+\mathbb{F}^{2}$, so that $X(m,n)(c)$ in the finitary endofunctor
world corresponds to $X(m,n)_{c}$ in the presheaf world, for
$c\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$. We think of $X(m,n)_{\mathbf{v}}$ (resp.\ $X(m,n)_{\mathbf{p}}$) as a
set of values (resp.\ programs) with $m$ potential free program
variables, and $n$ potential free value variables.
\par Since abstraction should bind a value variable, the syntax
$$\begin{array}[]{rcll}e,f&::=&e\ f\mathrel{|}v\\
v&::=&x\mathrel{|}\lambda x.e\end{array}$$is thus
specified by
\begin{center}$\Sigma_{0}(X)(m,n)(\mathbf{p})=X(m,n)(\mathbf{p})^{2}+X(m,n)(\mathbf{v})$ \hfil and \hfil$\Sigma_{0}(X)(m,n)(\mathbf{v})=X(m,n+1)(\mathbf{p})$.
\end{center}A model $X$ of the syntax should thus in particular feature
operations
\begin{center}$\mathrm{abs}_{m,n}\colon X(m,n+1)(\mathbf{p})\rightarrow X(m,n)(\mathbf{v})$ \hfil$\mathrm{app}_{m,n}\colon X(m,n)(\mathbf{p})^{2}\rightarrow X(m,n)(\mathbf{p})$ \hfil$\mathrm{val}_{m,n}\colon X(m,n)(\mathbf{v})\rightarrow X(m,n)(\mathbf{p})$,
\end{center}where the last operation requires that values should embed into
programs.
\par\nota We implicitly view any $X\in[2\cdot\mathbb{F}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ as (some fixed, global
choice of) the corresponding functor $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}$. In
particular, we write $X(K)$, for any $K\in\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}$. Accordingly, we
view pairs $(m,n)$ as objects of $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}$. E.g., in this sense,
$(m,n+1)$ is isomorphic to $(m,n)+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}}$, where $\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}}$ denotes
the Yoneda embedding of $\mathbf{v}$ along $2\rightarrow\mathbb{F}^{2}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{2}$. So the arity
for abstraction in fact yields an operation
$X(K+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}})(\mathbf{p})\rightarrow X(K)(\mathbf{v})$.
Denoting composition of finitary endofunctors by $\otimes$, we define a
pointed strength for $\Sigma_{0}$ as follows. For any $X\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$,
$Y\in I/\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{0}}$, and $K\in\mathbb{F}^{2}$:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@at $\mathbf{p}$, we have
$$(\Sigma_{0}(X)\otimes Y)(K)(\mathbf{p})=X(Y(K))(\mathbf{p})^{2}+X(Y(K))(\mathbf{v})=\Sigma_{0}(X\otimes Y)(K)(\mathbf{p})\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$so we take $st_{X,Y,K,\mathbf{p}}$ to be the identity;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@at $\mathbf{v}$, we have
\begin{center}$(\Sigma_{0}(X)\otimes Y)(K)(\mathbf{v})=X(Y(K)+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}})(\mathbf{p})$ \hfil and \hfil$\Sigma_{0}(X\otimes Y)(K)(\mathbf{v})=X(Y(K+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}}))(\mathbf{p})\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$
\end{center}so we define $st_{X,Y,K,\mathbf{p}}$ by applying
$X(-)(\mathbf{p})$ to the copairing of $Y(K)\rightarrow Y(K+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}})$ and
$$\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}}\rightarrow I(K+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}})\rightarrow Y(K+\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{v}}).$$\end{itemize}\par We then specify transitions, which we first recall:
\begin{equation*}\frac{}{\lambda x_{1}.e\Downarrow e}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow e^{\prime}_{1}\quad e_{2}\Downarrow e^{\prime}_{2}\quad e^{\prime}_{1}[\lambda x_{1}.e^{\prime}_{2}]\Downarrow e_{3}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow e_{3}}~\cdot\end{equation*}\begin{rem}Here, we adopt the same convention as in the categorical
picture, where terms are implicitly considered as indexed over
sets, say $\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$, of potential free variables.
Furthermore, the evaluation relation again relates closed terms
to terms over one potential free variable $x_{1}$.
\end{rem}In order to specify such transitions, we take $\mathbb{C}_{1}=1$, as in the
call-by-name case, with $\mathbf{s}$ and $\mathbf{t}$ mapping the unique
object to $(0,0)_{\mathbf{p}}$ and $(0,1)_{\mathbf{p}}$, respectively: transitions will
relate a closed program to a program with one value variable
(morally the body of the obtained abstraction). For any
$X\in\mathbf{C}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta\cong\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}/\Delta$, We take $\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)$ to be the
coproduct $$\Sigma_{1}^{F}(X)=X_{0}(0,1)+A_{\beta_{v}}(X)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$where
$A_{\beta_{v}}(X)$ denotes the set of valid premises for the second rule,
i.e., triples $(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})\in X_{1}$ such that
$$r_{3}\cdot s_{\Downarrow}=(r_{1}\cdot t_{\Downarrow})[\lambda(r_{2}\cdot t_{\Downarrow})].$$\par Familiality of the induced functor $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{1}}/\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}$ follows
similarly to the call-by-name case, from the fact that $A_{\beta_{v}}(X)$ is isomorphic
to $[E_{\beta_{v}},X]$, where $E_{\beta_{v}}$ denotes the following pushout.

bisimilarity will follow if we can prove that boundary arities

cell complexes. This is again trivial for the first rule, while
for the second one we obtain the following morphism, which is a
relative cell complex by construction.

\end{center}\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Erratic non-determinism}
In this section, we consider the non-deterministic $\lambda$-calculus
investigated in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DavideLazy}{}{}, \lx@sectionsign 7]}. Its syntax is that of pure
$\lambda$-calculus, augmented with a unary operation $\uplus$, and its reduction
rules~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DavideLazy}{}{}, on pages 125 and 142]} are
\begin{equation*}\frac{}{{{\uplus}e}\Rightarrow e}\frac{}{{{\uplus}e}\Rightarrow\Omega}\frac{}{(\lambda x.e)\ f\Rightarrow e[f]}\\
\frac{e_{1}\Rightarrow e_{3}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Rightarrow e_{3}\ e_{2}}\frac{}{e\Rightarrow e}\frac{e_{1}\Rightarrow e_{2}\quad e_{2}\Rightarrow e_{3}}{e_{1}\Rightarrow e_{3}},\end{equation*}where $\Omega$ denotes any diverging term.
\par Let us start by giving a big-step presentation of this language. We
consider a labelled transition relation, i.e., we have two transition
relations $\Downarrow_{\lambda}$ (between a closed term and a term with one free
variable, as before) and $\Downarrow_{\tau}$ (between closed terms), inductively
generated by the following rules.
\begin{equation*}\frac{}{{{\uplus}e}\Downarrow_{\tau}e}\frac{}{{{\uplus}e}\Downarrow_{\tau}\Omega}\frac{}{\lambda x.e\Downarrow_{\lambda}e}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}\quad e_{3}[e_{2}]\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{4}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{4}}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}\quad e_{3}[e_{2}]\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{4}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{4}}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{3}}{e_{1}\ e_{2}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{3}\ e_{2}}\frac{}{e\Downarrow_{\tau}e}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{2}\quad e_{2}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{3}}{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{3}}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{2}\quad e_{2}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}}{e_{1}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}}~\cdot\end{equation*}\par We have:
\begin{prop}A relation is an applicative bisimulation in Sangiorgi's sense, say
a \emph{Sangiorgi bisimulation}, iff its open extension is a
substitution-closed bisimulation with the new rules.
\end{prop}\begin{proof}This is an easy corollary of the following lemma.
\end{proof}\begin{lem}For all closed $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$, and $e_{3}$ with one potential free variable, we have
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$e_{1}\Rightarrow e_{2}$ iff $e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}e_{2}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$e_{1}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$ iff $e_{1}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}$.
\end{itemize}\end{lem}\begin{proof}\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@All reduction rules also occur as some new rule for $\Downarrow_{\tau}$,
except the $\beta$-rule, which is easily derivable. We thus have
${\Rightarrow}\subseteq{\Downarrow_{\tau}}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Similarly, if $e_{1}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$, then by the previous point
$e_{1}\Downarrow_{\tau}\lambda(e_{3})$, hence by the last rule $e_{1}\Downarrow_{\lambda}e_{3}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Finally, let us prove both converse statements in one go by
induction on the transition proof.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@The first two axioms also are axioms in the original rules, hence easy.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For the third axiom, we are given $\lambda(e)\Downarrow_{\lambda}e$, hence
clearly $\lambda(e)\Rightarrow\lambda(e)$ as desired.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For the first $\beta$ rule, $e_{1}=e_{4}\ e_{5}$, and we know by
induction hypothesis that $e_{4}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{6})$ and $e_{6}[e_{5}]\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$. We
thus get $e_{4}\ e_{5}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{6})\ e_{5}\Rightarrow e_{6}[e_{5}]\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$, hence the
desired result.
\par\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The second $\beta$ rule is similar, except that we get a chain
$e_{4}\ e_{5}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{6})\ e_{5}\Rightarrow e_{6}[e_{5}]\Rightarrow e_{2}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The next three rules also occur as original rules, hence are
easily dealt with by induction hypothesis.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For the last rule, we have by induction hypothesis $e_{1}\Rightarrow e_{4}$
and $e_{4}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$, hence $e_{1}\Rightarrow\lambda(e_{3})$, as desired. \end{itemize}\end{itemize}\end{proof}\par The syntax is easily modelled by taking
$\Sigma_{0}(X)(n)=X(n+1)+X(n)^{2}+X(n)$, and the new rules are easily seen
to fit into a $\Sigma_{1}$ such that $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ preserves functional
bisimulations by Corollary~\ref{cor:cellularenough} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:cellscof}. Finally, substitution-closed
bisimilarity in the initial model coincides with Sangiorgi's
applicative bisimilarity, so we again deduce congruence of applicative
bisimilarity by Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Howe's format}
In this section, we show that, up to suitable encoding, our framework
covers languages complying with a format proposed by Howe~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96}{}{}, Lemma
6.1]} --- or rather a slight variant
thereof (see Remark~\ref{rk:discrepance-howe} below). We first introduce
the format, and then explain how to embed it into our framework. The
format illustrates in which sense cellularity is in particular an
acyclicity condition. Furthermore, it would be easy, but much more
verbose, to extend the format to a simply-typed setting; we refrain
from doing so in this already quite long paper.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Recalling Howe's format}
Regarding syntax, Howe's framework is parameterised by the choice
between call-by-name and call-by-value. His signatures are then much
like standard binding signatures~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{BindingSignatures}{}{}]}. We model
this in a setting similar to the call-by-value setting
of~\lx@sectionsign\ref{ss:cbv}, except that this time we build into the base
category the fact that values embed into terms. Specifically, we work
with the monoidal category $[\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}}]_{f}\simeq[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$, where $\mathbb{2}$
denotes the walking arrow category $\mathbf{v}\xrightarrow{\iota}\mathbf{p}$. We think of
an object of the base category $\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$, which is a pair $(s,f\colon m\rightarrow n)$
with $s\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$, as the index of terms of sort $s$, with $m$ value
variables and $n$ program variables, each $f(i)$ being thought as the
program counterpart of $i\in m$.
\par\par Let us first explain how the syntactic part of Howe's format may be
understood in terms of pointed strong endofunctors. Howe's notion of
syntactic signature encodes a choice between call-by-value and
call-by-name, through the choice of a distinguished sort, $\mathbf{v}$ or $\mathbf{p}$.
\nota \ \hfill\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@Given $m,n\in\mathbb{F}$ and $s\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$,
we denote any object $(s,(m\xrightarrow{f}n))$ of $\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$ by
$(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}$,
and the particular morphism $(\iota,\id)\colon(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}\rightarrow(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}}$ by $\iota$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Given $m,n\in\mathbb{F}$, we denote the object $(m\xrightarrow{in_{1}}m+n)$
of $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$ by $(m,n)$. Otherwise said, we treat the corresponding
embedding $\mathbb{F}^{2}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$ as an implicit coercion.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Accordingly, for any $m,n\in\mathbb{F}$ and $s\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$, we denote
$(m\xrightarrow{in_{1}}m+n)_{s}$ by $(m,n)_{s}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Given $T\colon\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$ and $s\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$, we denote by
$T_{s}\colon\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$ the functor mapping $(m\xrightarrow{f}n)$ to $T(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}$.
\end{itemize}\begin{rem}Through the equivalence $[\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}}]_{f}\simeq[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$,
composition of endofunctors becomes a monoidal product
defined by
$$(F\otimes G)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}=\Lan_{J}(F_{s})(G(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}\xrightarrow{G\iota}G(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}})\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$where $J:\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}}$ is the
canonical embedding. The unit $I$ is defined
by $$I(n_{\mathbf{v}}\xrightarrow{f}n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}=n_{s}.$$for any object
$(n_{\mathbf{v}}\xrightarrow{f}n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}$. Intuitively, $I$ merely returns the set
of variables of each sort.
\end{rem}Howe distinguishes value operations
from program operations:
\defi
A \emph{Howe binding signature} consists of
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a \emph{binding sort} $s_{v}\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a set $O_{\mathbf{p}}$ of \emph{program operations}, equipped with
a map $N^{\mathbf{p}}\colon O_{\mathbf{p}}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ and a family
$d^{\mathbf{p}}\in\prod_{o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}}\mathbb{N}^{N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a set $O_{\mathbf{v}}$ of \emph{value operations}, equipped with two maps
$N^{+}\colon O_{\mathbf{v}}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ and $N^{-}\colon O_{\mathbf{v}}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$, and a family
$d^{-}\in\prod_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}\mathbb{N}^{N^{-}_{o}}$.
\end{itemize}\begin{terminology}For any operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}$ (resp.\ $O_{\mathbf{v}}$), the sequence
$(d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,1},\ldots,d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}})$ (resp.\ $(0,\ldots,0,d^{-}_{o,1},\ldots,d^{-}_{o,N^{-}_{o}})$, with $N^{+}_{o}$ leading $0$s) is called the
\emph{(binding) arity} of $o$.
Typically, $\lambda$-abstraction and pairing are value operations.
The numbers $N^{+}_{o}$ and $N^{-}_{o}$ respectively
count
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@\emph{active} arguments which should be evaluated before
reaching a value, as both arguments of the pairing operation, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@\emph{passive} arguments which are not evaluated until the
operation is destroyed, as the argument of a $\lambda$-abstraction.
\end{itemize}Active arguments are not allowed to bind any variable, hence the
absence of a family $d^{+}$ in signatures.
\end{terminology}\par Despite their name, value operations may or may not return values,
depending on the status of their arguments: a pair $\langle e_{1},e_{2}\rangle$ is only a
value when both $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are. In order to generate the right
syntax in our strongly-sorted setting, we need to introduce two
incarnations of each value operation, one for constructing values, the
other for constructing programs.
Any Howe binding signature generates a pointed
strong endofunctor, as follows. We first define an auxiliary
operation for adding bound variables in the right component --- as
prescribed by the binding sort $s_{v}$.
\nota
For any $(m\xrightarrow{f}n)\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$, $p\in\mathbb{F}$, and $s\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$ let
$(m\xrightarrow{f}n)+_{s}p$ denote
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$(m+p\xrightarrow{f+\id_{p}}n+p)$ if $s=\mathbf{v}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$(m\xrightarrow{f}n\hookrightarrow n+p)$ if $s=\mathbf{p}$.
\end{itemize}\defi Given any Howe binding signature $B$, the \emph{generated}
endofunctor $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$ on $[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ is defined by
$$\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Sigma_{0}^{B}(F)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}&=&\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}F((m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}})^{N^{+}_{o}}\times\prod_{i\in N^{-}_{o}}F((m\xrightarrow{f}n)+_{s_{v}}d^{-}_{o,i})_{\mathbf{p}}\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}\\
\Sigma_{0}^{B}(F)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}}&=&\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}F((m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}})^{N^{+}_{o}}\times\prod_{i\in N^{-}_{o}}F((m\xrightarrow{f}n)+_{s_{v}}d^{-}_{o,i})_{\mathbf{p}}\\
&&{}+\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}}\prod_{i\in N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}F((m\xrightarrow{f}n)+_{s_{v}}d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,i})_{\mathbf{p}}\end{array}$$for all $F\in[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ and $m,n\in\mathbb{F}$, with obvious action on morphisms.
We now want to express $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$ as a familial functor.
For this, we start by defining
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a functor $A^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}\colon{\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}}^{\mathit{op}}\rightarrow[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ for
each program operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a functor $A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}\colon{(\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}\rightarrow[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ for
each value operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$,
\end{itemize}in such a way that $\Sigma_{0}^{B}(F)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}=\sum_{o}[A^{s}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n),F]$.
\defi
Given any Howe binding signature,
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@for any program operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}$, let the \emph{arity}
of $o$ be the functor $A^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}\colon{(\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}\rightarrow[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$
mapping $(m\xrightarrow{f}n)$ to the coproduct of representable presheaves
$$A^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)=\sum_{i\in N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}\mathbf{y}_{((m\ \xrightarrow{f}\ n)+_{s_{v}}d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,i})_{\mathbf{p}}}\hbox to0.0pt{;\hss}$$\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@for any value operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, let the \emph{arity} of $o$ be the
functor $A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}\colon{(\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}\rightarrow[2\cdot\mathbb{F},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ mapping any object $(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}$
to the coproduct of representable presheaves
$$A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}=N^{+}_{o}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s}}+\sum_{i\in N^{-}_{o}}\mathbf{y}_{((m\xrightarrow{f}n)+_{s_{v}}d^{-}_{o,i})_{\mathbf{p}}}.$$\end{itemize}\begin{rem}The arity functors are contravariant because the Yoneda embedding
is, for covariant presheaves.
\end{rem}By construction:
\begin{prop}The endofunctor $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$ is familial, with
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@as spectrum the functor
$$S^{B}\cong\Sigma_{0}^{B}(1)\cong O_{\mathbf{p}}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{(0\rightarrow 0)_{\mathbf{p}}}+O_{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{(0\rightarrow 0)_{\mathbf{v}}}\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$i.e.,
$$\begin{array}[t]{rcl}S^{B}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}}&=&O_{\mathbf{p}}+O_{\mathbf{v}}\\
S^{B}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}&=&O_{\mathbf{v}}\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}\end{array}$$with obvious action on morphisms,
so that $$\el(S^{B})=O_{\mathbf{p}}\cdot{(\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}+O_{\mathbf{v}}\cdot{(\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@and as exponent the functor $E^{B}\colon\el(S^{B})\rightarrow[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$
defined as the cotupling
$$[[A^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}]_{o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}},[A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}]_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}].$$\end{itemize}\end{prop}\begin{proof}By mere calculation, using the Yoneda lemma.
\end{proof}\par\par\begin{cor}We have, for all $F\in[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]_{f}$ and $(m\xrightarrow{f}n)\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}$,
$$\Sigma_{0}^{B}(F)((m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}})\cong\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}}[A^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n),F]+\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}[A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}},F]$$and $$\Sigma_{0}^{B}(F)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}\cong\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}}[A^{\mathbf{v}}_{o}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}},F].$$\end{cor}\par\par We now describe the syntax generated by $B$.
\par Let $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}$ be the monad induced by the monadic forgetful functor
$\Sigma_{0}^{B}\Mon\rightarrow[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$.
\par In order to define the format, we need to unfold $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(K)$, for $K$ a
coproduct of representable presheaves of the form $\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}}$.
For a single such presheaf, by Proposition~\ref{prop:freelambda},
$\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}})=\mu A.(I+\Sigma_{0}^{B}(A)+\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}}\otimes A)$. Unfolding
the definition of tensor product
(Remark~\ref{rk:howe-format-mon-prod}), noticing that the hom-set
$[s,s^{\prime}]$
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@is empty iff $s=\mathbf{p}$ and $s^{\prime}=\mathbf{v}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@is otherwise a singleton,
\end{itemize}we obtain the following result.
\par\par\begin{prop}We have, for all $n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}},m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $s,s^{\prime}\in\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$,
$A\colon\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$, and $f\colon m\rightarrow n$:
$$\begin{array}[]{rcl}(\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}}\otimes A)(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{s^{\prime}}&\cong&[s,s^{\prime}]\times A^{n_{\mathbf{p}}}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}}\times A^{n_{\mathbf{v}}}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}\\
&\cong&\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\emptyset&\mbox{if $s=\mathbf{p}$ and $s^{\prime}=\mathbf{v}$}\\
A^{n_{\mathbf{p}}}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{p}}\times A^{n_{\mathbf{v}}}(m\xrightarrow{f}n)_{\mathbf{v}}&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\end{array}$$\end{prop}\begin{rem}Intuitively, this will entail that $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}})$ extends the
syntax generated by $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$ with a new operation taking $n_{\mathbf{p}}$ programs
and $n_{\mathbf{v}}$ values as arguments, and returning a program or a value,
depending on $s$. As usual, if the output is a value, by action of
$\iota$, there is a corresponding program operation.
\end{rem}\par We now describe $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(K)$, for $K$ any coproduct of representable presheaves
of the form $\mathbf{y}_{(n_{\mathbf{v}},n_{\mathbf{p}})_{s}}$.
Let us first introduce some notations.
\defi
A {family of operation arities} is a family
$c=(m_{i},n_{i},s_{i})_{i\in I}$ of triples $(m_{i},n_{i},s_{i})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\times\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{p}\}$.
\nota
We think of any such triple $c_{i}=(m_{i},n_{i},s_{i})$ as an operation
$c_{i}\colon\mathbf{v}^{m_{i}}\times\mathbf{p}^{n_{i}}\rightarrow s_{i}$, hence denote any such family by
$(c_{i}\colon\mathbf{v}^{m_{i}}\times\mathbf{p}^{n_{i}}\rightarrow s_{i})_{i\in I}$.
We in fact extend this notation by
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@writing $\mathbf{v}^{m}\times\mathbf{p}^{n}\times s^{q}$,
to denote either $\mathbf{v}^{m+q}\times\mathbf{p}^{n}$, when $s=\mathbf{v}$, or $\mathbf{v}^{m}\times\mathbf{p}^{n+q}$, when
$s=\mathbf{p}$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@omitting $-^{n}$ if $n=0$ in the above product, e.g.,
$\mathbf{v}^{m}\rightarrow s$ denotes $\mathbf{v}^{m}\times\mathbf{p}^{0}\rightarrow s$, and finally
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@writing $c\colon s$ for $c\colon\mathbf{v}^{0}\times\mathbf{p}^{0}\rightarrow s$.
\end{itemize}We furthermore denote the disjoint union of families of operation
arities $K$ and $L$ by $K+L$. Given a family
$K=(c_{i}\colon\mathbf{v}^{m_{i}}\times\mathbf{p}^{n_{i}}\rightarrow s_{i})_{i}$ of operation arities, we also
denote by $K$ the coproduct of representable presheaves
$\sum_{i}\mathbf{y}_{(m_{i},n_{i})_{s_{i}}}\colon\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}}\rightarrow\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}$.
\begin{rem}By Notation~\ref{not:pluss}, for $m,n,p\in\mathbb{F}$, $(m,n)+_{s}p$ denotes
$(m+p,n)$ if $s=\mathbf{v}$, and $(m,n+p)$ otherwise.
\end{rem}We now give an inductive description of $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(K)$ on objects
of the form $(m,n)_{s}$ (Notation~\ref{not:pluss}).
Letting $m,n\vdash_{K}e:s$ mean that $e\in\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(K)(m,n)_{s}$, for a family $K$ of operation arities,
the free $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$-monoid over $K$ is inductively generated on objects of
the form $(m,n)_{s}$ by the following rules.
\begin{equation*}\frac{}{m,n\vdash_{K}x_{i}^{s}:s}~(i\in m)\frac{}{m,n\vdash_{K}a_{i}:\mathbf{p}}~(i\in n)\frac{m,n\vdash_{K}e_{1}:\mathbf{v}\quad\ldots\quad m,n\vdash_{K}e_{m^{\prime}}:\mathbf{v}\quad\quad m,n\vdash_{K}f_{1}:\mathbf{p}\quad\ldots\quad m,n\vdash_{K}f_{n^{\prime}}:\mathbf{p}}{m,n\vdash_{K}k(e_{1},\ldots,e_{m^{\prime}};f_{1},\ldots,f_{n^{\prime}}):s}~((k\colon\mathbf{v}^{m^{\prime}}\times\mathbf{p}^{n^{\prime}}\rightarrow s)\in K)\\
\frac{(m,n)+_{s_{v}}d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,1}\vdash_{K}e_{1}:\mathbf{p}\quad\ldots\quad(m,n)+_{s_{v}}d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}\vdash_{K}e_{N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}:\mathbf{p}}{m,n\vdash_{K}o(e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}}):\mathbf{p}}~(o\in O_{\mathbf{p}})\frac{m,n\vdash_{K}e_{1}:s\quad\ldots\quad m,n\vdash_{K}e_{N^{+}_{o}}:s\quad\quad(m,n)+_{s_{v}}d^{-}_{o,1}\vdash_{K}f_{1}:\mathbf{p}\quad\ldots\quad(m,n)+_{s_{v}}d^{-}_{o,N^{-}_{o}}\vdash_{K}f_{N^{-}_{o}}:\mathbf{p}}{m,n\vdash_{K}o_{s}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{+}_{o}};f_{1},\ldots,f_{N^{-}_{o}}):s}~(o\in O_{\mathbf{v}})\end{equation*}\begin{rem}Program operations $o\in O_{\mathbf{p}}$ only have one list of arguments.
Furthermore, they always return programs, so there is no need to
annotate them. By contrast, value operations $o^{\prime}\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$ have two
lists of arguments (active and passive arguments, see
Terminology~\ref{term:howesignatures}), and may return values or
programs, depending on the status of their active arguments. Thus,
e.g., any unannotated operation application $o(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})$ must be a
program operation application, while any annontated operation
application $o_{s}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{m};f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})$ must be a value operation
application.
\end{rem}\par The action on morphisms is straightforward: for renaming, we rename
(value and program) variables accordingly; for $\iota$, we replace each
$x_{i}^{\mathbf{v}}$ (resp.\ $o_{\mathbf{v}}$) with $x_{i}^{\mathbf{p}}$ (resp.\ $o_{\mathbf{p}}$). For morphisms
$K\rightarrow L$, we proceed similarly.
\par\begin{terminology}We think of elements $k$ from $K$ as \emph{metavariables}, while terms
of the form $a_{i}$ or $x_{i}^{s}$ are mere \emph{variables}.
\end{terminology}\nota\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@Following~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DBLP:conf/aplas/Hamana04}{}{}]}, for any $(k\colon\mathbf{v}^{m}\times\mathbf{p}^{n}\rightarrow s)\in K$, we abbreviate
$k(x_{1}^{\mathbf{v}},\ldots,x_{m}^{\mathbf{v}};a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})$ to just $k$ when $(m,n)$ is clear
from context.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For value operations $o$, we sometimes omit the subscript
$s$ in $o_{s}(\ldots)$, when the expected sort is clear from context.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Similarly, we sometimes omit the exponent $s$ in variables $x_{i}^{s}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@In metavariable application
$k(e_{1},\ldots,e_{m^{\prime}};f_{1},\ldots,f_{n^{\prime}})$, as well as in value
operation application $o(e_{1},\ldots,e_{p};f_{1},\ldots,f_{q})$, when one sequence is
empty we omit it altogether, writing, e.g., $k(e_{1},\ldots,e_{m^{\prime}})$ or
$o(f_{1},\ldots,f_{q})$. When both lists are empty we simply write $k$, resp.\ $o$.
\end{itemize}Thus, e.g., $k$ may denote a nullary metavariable, or a non-nullary
metavariable with identity substitution.
\par Let us now introduce Howe's notion of signature for evaluation rules,
restricting attention to signatures satisfying the syntactic condition
of~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96}{}{}, Lemma 6.1]}. Evaluation is a
binary relation between closed programs and closed values. By
default, all value operations $o$ are considered as coming equipped
with their \emph{canonical} evaluation rule
\begin{equation}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow v_{1}\quad\ldots\quad e_{N^{+}_{o}}\Downarrow v_{N^{+}_{o}}}{o_{\mathbf{p}}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{+}_{o}};f_{1},\ldots,f_{N^{-}_{o}})\Downarrow o_{\mathbf{v}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}};f_{1},\ldots,f_{N^{-}_{o}})~\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}}\end{equation}\par Howe's signatures thus only need to specify evaluation of program
operations. We now successively introduce notions of premises, rules,
and signatures.
\par We start by fixing a global choice of finite coproducts in both
$[2\cdot\mathbb{N}^{2},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ (families of operation arities) $[\mathbb{2}\cdot\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$
(presheaves).
\par\defi Given any families $K$ and $L$ of operation arities,
a \emph{premise} $K\rightarrow L$
consists of a \emph{source} program $0,0\vdash_{K}e:\mathbf{p}$
and a \emph{target} value $0,0\vdash_{L}v:\mathbf{v}$, where
$L$ and $v$ take one of the following two forms:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@either $L=K+(c\colon\mathbf{v})$, extending $K$ with one closed value
metavariable,
in which case $v=c$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@or $L=K+(\alpha_{i}\colon\mathbf{v})_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N^{+}_{o}\}}+(\beta_{i}\colon s_{v}^{d^{-}_{o,i}}\rightarrow\mathbf{p})_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N^{-}_{o}\}}$
for some value operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, in
which case the target is $o_{\mathbf{v}}(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{N^{+}_{o}};\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{N^{-}_{o}})$.
\end{itemize}\nota We write any premise $(e,v)\colon K\rightarrow L$ as $K\xrightarrow{e\Downarrow v}L$.
\defi
A \emph{rule} consists of
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a \emph{head} program operation $o$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a composable sequence of premises
$K_{0}\xrightarrow{e_{1}\Downarrow v_{1}}K_{1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow K_{q-1}\xrightarrow{e_{q}\Downarrow v_{q}}K_{q}$,
where $K_{0}=(k_{i}\colon s_{v}^{d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,i}}\rightarrow\mathbf{p})_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}\}}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a \emph{tail} metavariable $(k_{v}\colon\mathbf{v})$ in $K_{q}$.
\end{itemize}A \emph{Howe dynamic signature} over a Howe binding signature is a
family of rules.
\nota Such a rule is denoted by
\begin{equation*}\frac{e_{1}\Downarrow v_{1}\quad\ldots\quad e_{q}\Downarrow v_{q}}{o(k_{1},\ldots,k_{N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}})\Downarrow k_{v}}\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}\end{equation*}The families of operation arities $K_{0},\ldots,K_{q}$ are left implicit.
\begin{rem}There are some discrepancies w.r.t.\ Howe's original
format~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DBLP:journals/iandc/Howe96}{}{}, Lemma 6.1]}.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@We restrict to rules with a finite number of premises.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@We have a slightly different treatment of value vs.\ program
variables and metavariables.
\end{itemize}\end{rem}\par\defi For any Howe binding signature $B$, and Howe dynamic signature
$D$ over it, the \emph{evaluation}, denoted by $\Downarrow^{B,D}$, or $\Downarrow$ for short,
is the binary relation between programs and values, obtained
inductively by instantiating the given rules together with the
canonical rules~\eqref{rules:canonical}.
Let us now recall Howe's general definition of applicative
bisimulation, and its open extension.
\defi
For any Howe binding signature $B$, and Howe dynamic signature $D$
over it, an \emph{applicative simulation} is a binary relation $R$
in $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}}$ over the injection $\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\emptyset)(0,0)_{\mathbf{v}}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\emptyset)(0,0)_{\mathbf{p}}$, such
that for any closed programs $e$ and $e^{\prime}$ such that
$e\mathrel{R_{\mathbf{p}}}e^{\prime}$, and any transition
$e\Downarrow o_{\mathbf{v}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}};e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}})$, there exist
$v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{N^{+}_{o}},e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}}$ and a transition
$e^{\prime}\Downarrow o_{\mathbf{v}}(v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{N^{+}_{o}};e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}})$, such that
$v_{i}\mathrel{R_{\mathbf{v}}}v^{\prime}_{i}$ for all $i\in N^{+}_{O}$, and
$e_{j}[\sigma]\mathrel{R_{\mathbf{p}}}e^{\prime}_{j}[\sigma]$, for all $j\in N^{-}_{o}$ and closing
substitutions $\sigma$.
\par An \emph{applicative bisimulation} is an applicative simulation
whose converse relation also is one.
\par Applicative bisimulations are closed under union, and we let
$\sim_{B,D}$, or $\sim$ for short, denote the largest one.
\par Finally, the open extension $R^{∘}$ of a relation $R$ is the largest
substitution-closed relation contained in $R$ on closed programs and
values.
\par\begin{rem}By definition, being a subobject of the injection
$$\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\emptyset)(0,0)_{\mathbf{v}}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{T}_{0}^{B}(\emptyset)(0,0)_{\mathbf{p}}$$in $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}^{\mathbb{2}}$, any applicative
simulation is such that for any related values $v\mathrel{R}_{\mathbf{v}}v^{\prime}$,
$v$ and $v^{\prime}$ should also be related as programs, i.e.,
$\iota\cdot v\mathrel{R}_{\mathbf{p}}\iota\cdot v^{\prime}$.
\end{rem}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Congruence by encoding in our framework}
We now want to prove using Theorem~\ref{thm:main} that $\sim^{∘}$ is a
congruence. For this, we could try to naively model evaluation rules
as a dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1}$ over $\Sigma_{0}^{B}$. However, substitution-closed
bisimilarity in the obtained system would not coincide with
applicative bisimilarity in Howe's sense. Furthermore, the induced
functor $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}\colon\Sigma_{0}^{B}\Trans\rightarrow\widehat{\mathbb{C}_{\mathbf{s}}}$ would not be
cellular. Indeed, consider for instance the usual, call-by-name rule
for application. In Howe's format, it gives the following:
\begin{equation*}\frac{k_{1}\Downarrow\lambda(k_{3})\quad k_{3}(k_{2})\Downarrow k_{4}}{k_{1}\ k_{2}\Downarrow k_{4}},\end{equation*}where all $k_{i}$ are metavariables.
\nota
For any $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we use the abbreviation
$n_{s}:=((0,0)+_{s_{v}}n)_{s}$ --- because we will mainly need tuples
$(n_{\mathbf{p}},n_{\mathbf{v}})$ with only $n_{s_{v}}\neq 0$ from now on.
Letting $E$ denote the exponent of the induced $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$, and $o$
denote the element corresponding to this rule in the spectrum, the
boundary arity $E(s_{\Downarrow}\upharpoonright o)\colon E(\mathbf{s}(\Downarrow),o\cdot s_{\Downarrow})\rightarrow E(\Downarrow,o)$ is the
bottom composite in the following diagram,

\end{center}where
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$\bar{\chi}$ is analogous to Definition~\ref{def:chibar};
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@we implicitly use transposition, the Yoneda lemma, and canonical
isomorphisms $\mathscr{L}(A)+\mathscr{L}(B)\cong\mathscr{L}(A+B)$.
\end{itemize}This bottom composite is not a relative cellular complex,
because $\lambda(k_{1})\colon\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{0_{\mathbf{v}}})\rightarrow\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{1_{\mathbf{p}}})$ is not of the form
$\mathscr{L}(\mathbf{y}_{s_{\Downarrow}})$.
\par So we have two problems: substitution-closed bisimilarity is not as
desired, and $\Sigma_{1}^{\mathbf{s}}$ is not cellular. The solution to both
problems is to rectify this last point. Namely, we construct a new
signature from the evaluation rules, in such a way that we may observe
each argument of a value. For this, we first need to generalise the
notions of premise, rule, and signature, as well as the evaluation
relation induced by a signature, which in turn requires us to
introduce the Howe context induced by a Howe dynamic signature over a
Howe binding signature.
\par We fix a Howe binding signature $B$ and a Howe dynamic signature $D$
over it for the rest of this section.
\defi
We define the \emph{Howe context} induced by $(B,D)$, as follows.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@For state types, we take $\mathbb{C}_{0}={(\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}})}^{\mathit{op}}$, with the
monoidal structure on $\hat{\mathbb{C}}_{0}=[\mathbb{2}\times\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{2}},\mathbf{S}\mathbf{e}\mathbf{t}]$ specified in
Remark~\ref{rk:howe-format-mon-prod}.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For transition types, we take $$\mathbb{C}_{1}=\{\Downarrow\}\uplus\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}},i\in N^{+}_{o}}\{\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}\}\uplus\sum_{o\in O_{\mathbf{v}},j\in N^{-}_{o}}\{\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}\}.$$\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@We define source and target as follows
\begin{center}$\begin{array}[]{rcl}\mathbf{s}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}&\rightarrow&\mathbb{C}_{0}\\
\Downarrow&\mapsto&0_{\mathbf{p}}\\
\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}&\mapsto&0_{\mathbf{v}}\\
\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}&\mapsto&0_{\mathbf{v}}\\
\end{array}$
\hskip 20.44434pt$\begin{array}[]{rcll}\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}&\rightarrow&\mathbb{C}_{0}\\
\Downarrow&\mapsto&0_{\mathbf{v}}\\
\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}&\mapsto&0_{\mathbf{v}}&\mbox{($o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, $i\in N^{+}_{o}$)}\\
\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}&\mapsto&(d^{-}_{o,j})_{\mathbf{p}}&\mbox{($o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, $j\in N^{-}_{o}$)}\\
\end{array}$
\end{center}\end{itemize}\par We now introduce the new notions of premise, rule, and dynamic
signature, which we deem \emph{rigid} to avoid confusion with the
original.
\defi
A \emph{rigid premise} consists of a family of operation arities $K$,
called the \emph{source type},
a transition type $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}_{1}$ and a \emph{source} term
$0,0\vdash_{K}e:\mathbf{s}(\alpha)$.
\par The \emph{target type} of a rigid premise $(K,\alpha,e)$ is the family
$L:=K+(k\colon s_{v}^{n}\rightarrow s)$, where $\mathbf{t}(\alpha)=n_{s}$, and its \emph{target} is the fresh
metavariable $k\colon s_{v}^{n}\rightarrow s\in L$.
\par We denote such a premise by $K\xrightarrow{e\mathrel{\alpha}k}L$.
\par\defi A \emph{rigid rule} consists of
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a \emph{head} program operation $o$,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a composable sequence of rigid premises
$K_{0}\xrightarrow{e_{1}\mathrel{\alpha_{1}}k_{1}}K_{1}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow K_{q-1}\xrightarrow{e_{p}\mathrel{\alpha_{q}}k_{q}}K_{q}$,
where $K_{0}=(k_{i}\colon s_{v}^{d^{\mathbf{p}}_{o,i}}\rightarrow\mathbf{p})_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N^{\mathbf{p}}_{o}\}}$, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a \emph{tail} metavariable $(k_{v}\colon\mathbf{v})$ in $K_{q}$.
\end{itemize}A \emph{rigid dynamic signature} over a Howe binding signature is a
family of rigid rules.
\par\defi The labelled transition system induced by $B$ any the rigid dynamic
signature $D^{\prime}$ is defined by instantiating the given rigid rules,
together with the canonical rules~\eqref{rules:canonical}, and the
following new rules.
\begin{equation}\frac{}{o_{\mathbf{v}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}};v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}})\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}v_{i}}\qquad\quad\frac{}{o_{\mathbf{v}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}};v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}})\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}v^{\prime}_{j}}~\cdot\end{equation}We may now define the rigid signature induced by $(B,D)$.
\par\defi Let the rigid dynamic signature $R(B,D)$ induced by $(B,D)$ be
obtained as follows. For each rule in $D$, $R(B,D)$ has a rule for
the same program operation, whose premises are obtained by replacing
each original premise
$K\xrightarrow{e\Downarrow o_{\mathbf{v}}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{N^{+}_{o}};k^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,k^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}})}L$ with any
linearisation (in the straightforward, suitable sense) of the
following tree.
\begin{center}\hbox to471.32pt{\vbox to143.81pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 235.65863pt\lower-19.6486pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-232.32562pt}{-9.07588pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\end{center}\par Let us show that the rigid signature $R(B,D)$ is adequate.
\begin{prop}The open extension of applicative bisimilarity in the sense of
$(B,D)$ coincides with substitution-closed bisimilarity in the
labelled transition system generated by $R(B,D)$.
\end{prop}\begin{proof}Let $\sim^{\prime}$ denote substitution-closed bisimilarity in the sense of
$R(B,D)$.
\par First of all, ${\sim^{∘}}$ is a substitution-closed bisimulation; indeed,
$\Downarrow$ is the same relation in both systems --- by a straightforward
induction --- and by definition of applicative bisimulation, for any
$o_{\mathbf{v}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}})\sim o_{\mathbf{v}}(v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{N^{+}_{o}},e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{N^{-}_{o}})$, we have $v_{i}\sim v^{\prime}_{i}$ and
$e_{j}\sim^{∘}e^{\prime}_{j}$, for all $i$ and $j$, which ensures that the new
transitions $\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}$ and $\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}$ are matched. Thus, we have
${\sim^{∘}}\subseteq{\sim^{\prime}}$.
\par Conversely, the new transitions ensure that ${\sim^{\prime}}$ is an applicative
bisimulation, hence is contained in $\sim$ on closed terms. But it is
substitution-closed, so we get ${\sim^{\prime}}\subseteq{\sim^{∘}}$, as desired.
\end{proof}\par Finally, we show that the rigid signature $R(B,D)$ straightforwardly
gives rise to a dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1}^{B,D}$, such that the initial
vertical $\Sigma_{1}^{B,D}$-algebra is isomorphic to the generated labelled
transition system, and furthermore that the induced functor
$(\Sigma^{B,D}_{1})^{\mathbf{s}}$ is cellular, hence that by
Proposition~\ref{prop:adequacy}, Corollary~\ref{cor:cellularenough},
and Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, $\sim^{∘}$ is a congruence.
\par\nota We tend to abbreviate $\Sigma_{1}^{B,D}$ to $\Sigma_{1}$, for readability.
\par Let us present the dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1}^{B,D}$, which will consist of
various components: one dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1,o}$ for each value
operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, describing both kinds of canonical
rules~\eqref{rules:canonical} and~\eqref{rules:new},
plus one dynamic signature $\Sigma_{1,r}$ for
each other rule.
\par\par\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@For each value operation $o\in O_{\mathbf{v}}$, we define
$$\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Sigma_{1,o}^{F}(X)(\Downarrow)&=&X(\Downarrow)^{N^{+}_{o}}\times\prod_{j\in N^{-}_{o}}X((d^{-}_{o,j})_{\mathbf{p}})\\
\Sigma_{1,o}^{F}(X)(\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i})&=&X(0_{\mathbf{v}})^{N^{+}_{o}}\times\prod_{j\in N^{-}_{o}}X((d^{-}_{o,j})_{\mathbf{p}})\\
\Sigma_{1,o}^{F}(X)(\Downarrow^{-}_{o,i})&=&X(0_{\mathbf{v}})^{N^{+}_{o}}\times\prod_{j\in N^{-}_{o}}X((d^{-}_{o,j})_{\mathbf{p}})\\
\end{array}$$with as
$\Sigma_{1,o}^{F}(X)\rightarrow\Sigma_{0}^{B}(X)\mathbf{s}\times X\mathbf{t}$:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@at $\Downarrow$: $(r_{1},\ldots,r_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}})\mapsto\begin{array}[t]{l}(in_{o_{\mathbf{p}}}(r_{1}\cdot s_{\Downarrow},\ldots,r_{N^{+}_{o}}\cdot s_{\Downarrow},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}}),\\
o_{\mathbf{v}}(r_{1}\cdot t_{\Downarrow},\ldots,r_{N^{+}_{o}}\cdot t_{\Downarrow},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}}))\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}\end{array}$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@at $\Downarrow^{+}_{o,i}$:
$(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}})\mapsto(in_{o_{\mathbf{v}}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}}),v_{i})\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@at $\Downarrow^{-}_{o,j}$:
$(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}})\mapsto(in_{o_{\mathbf{v}}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{+}_{o}},e_{1},\ldots,e_{N^{-}_{o}}),e_{j})\hbox to0.0pt{.\hss}$
\end{itemize}\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For each rigid premise $p=(K\xrightarrow{e\mathrel{\alpha}k}L)$,
we define the cospan induced by $p$ to be
$$\mathscr{L}(K)\xrightarrow{\ell}E_{p}\xleftarrow{r}\mathscr{L}(L)\hbox to0.0pt{,\hss}$$where the left-hand morphism $\ell$ is defined by the pushout
\begin{equation}\hbox to209.93pt{\vbox to50.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 104.96515pt\lower-26.06439pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{
